A scheme that encrypts but does not authenticate lets an attacker modify ciphertext, so an application must verify before acting on it.
Storing a symmetric key next to the data it protects provides no real confidentiality if the same storage is compromised.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the scheme provides integrity as well as confidentiality, because one alone is rarely enough.
Look for nonce or initialisation vector generation and confirm it cannot repeat.
Check where the key is stored and who can read it.
Notice any custom cipher or mode, which is a finding on its own.
defensive: Use an authenticated encryption mode from a standard library rather than combining primitives yourself.
Derive keys with a key derivation function, not by hashing a passphrase directly.
Never reuse a nonce with the same key, and prefer constructions that fail safely if one might repeat.
Store keys in a dedicated secret store with restricted access, and separate them from the data they protect.
Plan for key rotation before you need it, and confirm the rotated key actually replaces the old one.

topics.name: Hashing, Salting and Password Storage
topics.description: Why passwords are stored as slow, salted hashes, exactly how a salt defeats precomputed tables, and how memory-hard functions change the attacker's economics.

content.overview: Password storage is the single most consequential use of hashing. Storing a fast hash is equivalent to storing the password, because an attacker can simply try guesses as fast as the hardware allows.
how_it_works: A general-purpose hash such as SHA-256 is designed to be fast, which is exactly wrong for password storage.
A password hash is deliberately slow and memory-hard, so each guess costs the attacker real time and memory.
A unique salt per password means two users with the same password get different stored values, and precomputed tables cannot be reused.
The salt is not secret and is stored alongside the hash, so it only needs to be unique rather than hidden.
Password hashing is deliberately not reversible: verifying a password means hashing the candidate and comparing.
history: Passwords were once stored in plaintext, and later with unsalted fast hashes, so one breach cracked every account at once.
Per-user salts fixed rainbow tables but did nothing against a fast hash, since guesses were still cheap.
Memory-hard algorithms such as Argon2, scrypt and bcrypt were introduced to make parallel and hardware attacks expensive.
Tuning the work factor is now expected, since a fixed cost becomes cheap as hardware improves.
real_world: A leaked database hashed with a fast algorithm has historically been cracked within hours on consumer hardware.
A single reused password across services is what turns one database leak into many account compromises.
A hard-coded work factor from years ago is now far too cheap, even though nothing in the code changed.
what_to_look_for: Identify the algorithm and confirm it is intended for passwords rather than general use.
Check that each user has a unique salt.
Check whether the work factor is set explicitly and is appropriate for current hardware.
Notice any password policy that pushes people toward short predictable patterns rather than long unique ones.
defensive: Use a memory-hard password hash with a unique per-user salt and a tuned work factor.
Never use a general-purpose hash for passwords, even with a salt, because the speed is the problem.
Require multi-factor authentication so a cracked password is not sufficient on its own.
Check new and changed passwords against a breached-password list.
Re-evaluate the work factor periodically, since hardware improves faster than code changes.

topics.name: Public-Key Cryptography and Key Exchange
topics.description: How a public and private key pair replaces a shared secret, how an ephemeral exchange produces a session key, and which two things it still does not authenticate.

content.overview: Public-key cryptography uses a mathematically linked pair of keys: one that can be published and one that cannot. It solved the key distribution problem that had limited symmetric encryption for decades.
how_it_works: Each user holds a private key that stays with them and a public key that anyone can have.
Data encrypted to your public key can only be decrypted with your private key.
A signature created with your private key can be verified by anyone holding your public key.
A key agreement protocol such as Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive one shared secret over an observed channel, without ever sending the secret.
The security rests on a mathematical problem being hard in one direction and easy in the other, which is why only reviewed curves and parameters are acceptable.
history: Public-key ideas appeared in classified work in the 1970s and were published by Diffie, Hellman and Rivest.
RSA became the dominant scheme for both encryption and signatures, and for a long time was also used with small parameters by mistake.
Elliptic-curve schemes offer equivalent strength with much smaller keys, which reduced handshake cost and is now the default in TLS.
Post-quantum schemes have been standardised for the future, because an adversary can record traffic today and decrypt it later.
real_world: A key exchange with a non-standard curve removes the assumption that discrete logarithms are hard, which can let an attacker recover the shared secret.
Traffic captured today can be decrypted in future if the algorithm used is broken later, which is why harvest-now-decrypt-later is a real concern.
An implementation that accepts any offered parameter can be coerced into choosing a weak one.
what_to_look_for: Confirm only standard curves and standard parameter sizes are accepted, with no negotiation downgrade path.
Check that keys are generated with a good random source rather than derived from predictable values.
Notice whether forward secrecy is claimed, since it decides whether a later key compromise exposes old traffic.
Check that key validation actually happens, since an unauthenticated handshake has no identity to trust.
defensive: Use well-reviewed algorithms from a maintained library, and avoid implementing the mathematics yourself.
Enable forward secrecy, commonly called ephemeral key exchange, so past traffic is not exposed by a later key theft.
Pin the set of acceptable parameters in configuration rather than trusting the peer to choose.
Plan a migration path to post-quantum key exchange for long-lived sensitive traffic.
Validate peer keys against something you already trust rather than accepting whatever is presented.

topics.name: Digital Signatures, Certificates and PKI
topics.description: How a signature proves origin and integrity, how a certificate binds a name to a public key, and how a chain back to a trusted root decides what a browser accepts.

content.overview: A digital signature proves a key holder authorised a specific piece of data. A certificate binds an identity to a public key, and the public key infrastructure is the chain of trust that says who is allowed to issue those certificates.
how_it_works: Signing hashes the data and encrypts the hash with a private key, so the signature is bound to that exact content.
Verification uses the public key to recover the signed hash and compares it with a fresh hash of the received data.
A certificate contains a public key, an identity, and a signature from an issuer, so a relying party can check who vouched for the key.
A trust store holds the roots the client is willing to accept, and the chain from leaf to root is what makes an untrusted certificate acceptable.
Validation checks chain, dates, permitted uses and revocation, and a client that skips a step gains nothing from the scheme.
history: Certificates were introduced with the public web because there was no way to know whom a public key belonged to.
Root certificates distributed with operating systems and browsers became the anchor of trust, and their compromise has repeatedly broken trust worldwide.
Certificate revocation has always been awkward, because a revoked certificate is a small amount of signed data that must be distributed reliably.
Certificate transparency was introduced to make issuance publicly auditable, so a mis-issued certificate can be spotted even before it is used.
real_world: A certificate issued to the wrong name can let an impersonating server pass validation, which is why name checking is essential.
A device clock that is far out of step makes perfectly valid certificates look expired, so time accuracy is a security control.
Ignoring a certificate warning trains users to accept interception, which is how warnings get defeated in practice.
what_to_look_for: Confirm the expected name is checked against the certificate, not just that a chain validates.
Check clock accuracy, since validation depends on it.
Check that warnings are treated as fatal rather than dismissible.
Look for internal certificates issued by a private authority, and confirm that authority is one you actually intend to trust.
defensive: Use certificates from a reputable authority and automate renewal, so expiry is never a manual step.
Validate the full chain, the name, the dates and the permitted uses, and fail closed on any problem.
Keep the trust store small and current, since every root in it can issue for every name you visit.
Use certificate transparency monitoring for your own domains to catch a mis-issuance quickly.
Treat a bypassed certificate warning as an incident, not as a user inconvenience.

topics.name: TLS: How a Secure Connection Is Negotiated
topics.description: Follow a TLS 1.3 handshake message by message: where the session keys come from, how the server proves its identity, and which checks a client must never skip.

content.overview: TLS is what makes HTTPS work. The handshake agrees on a protocol version, authenticates the server, negotiates keys, and only then does application data flow. Almost every step is a decision about what you refuse to accept.
how_it_works: The client offers a list of protocol versions and cipher suites, and the server chooses one from that list.
Server certificates are presented and validated, which is how the client learns it is talking to the right host.
A key exchange derives fresh session secrets, so each connection has keys that are never transmitted.
With modern versions the key exchange can itself be authenticated, so no separate certificate round trip is needed.
Finished messages verify that both sides derived the same keys and detected tampering, before any application data is sent.
history: SSL was designed for the web in the 1990s and had a long list of design and implementation problems.
TLS 1.2 improved on it but still allowed negotiation to fall back to weaker options, which is what downgrade attacks exploited.
TLS 1.3 removed the problematic negotiation, shortened the handshake, and removed algorithms that were long known to be weak.
Encrypted client hello, now being adopted, hides the last plaintext detail, which was the server name in the initial request.
real_world: A server that still supports an old protocol version remains downgradeable even if modern clients prefer a new one.
A captive portal that intercepts traffic typically presents a certificate the client is asked to accept, which is the moment trust is given away.
Certificate pinning left in place after a key rotation causes an outage that is often mistaken for an attack.
what_to_look_for: Check that only current protocol versions are enabled and that weak cipher suites are removed.
Confirm the server presents a certificate for the exact name being visited.
Check that forward secrecy is in use and that legacy renegotiation is disabled.
Check the certificate chain is complete, because an incomplete chain fails for some clients and not others.
defensive: Enable only current protocol versions and a short list of strong cipher suites.
Serve HSTS so browsers refuse to fall back to an unencrypted connection.
Automate certificate issuance and renewal, including the intermediate certificates.
Monitor for protocol downgrade attempts and for clients reporting certificate errors.
Remove obsolete options such as legacy renegotiation, which exist for compatibility nobody should still need.

topics.name: Random Numbers, Nonces and Weak Entropy
topics.description: Cryptography fails quietly when randomness is predictable: where entropy comes from, the exact job a nonce does, and how a crippled generator destroys key strength.

content.overview: Much of modern security depends on values nobody should be able to predict. Weak randomness in the wrong place does not reduce security slightly; it removes it completely for that mechanism.
how_it_works: A cryptographic random number generator should be indistinguishable from random to an observer who has seen no previous outputs.
Operating system generators are seeded from hardware entropy sources and are suitable for keys, nonces and salts.
A general-purpose random function in a programming language is often predictable, and was the root cause of many real vulnerabilities.
A nonce must be unique for a given key, which is a different requirement from being random, and is usually easier to guarantee.
A unique nonce can be a counter, and a counter is easier to reason about than a random value you hope does not collide.
history: Early software seeded generators with the current time, which made keys guessable to anyone who knew roughly when the system booted.
A small change in initialisation values in a widely used cryptography library had an outsized effect, and the incident changed how randomness is reviewed.
Randomness requirements became formal, with standards specifying how randomness should be obtained and tested.
Hardware and virtualised environments made accidental weak entropy easier to introduce, since a virtual machine can start repeatedly from similar state.
real_world: Predictable session identifiers let an attacker fix a session before a victim ever logs in, which is why session generation is security-critical.
A virtual machine restored from a snapshot can start with the same generator state, so keys created after a restore can repeat.
Predictable password-reset tokens turn a forgotten password into an account takeover.
what_to_look_for: Check that keys, nonces, tokens and identifiers all come from a cryptographic source, not a general-purpose one.
Look for time-based seeding anywhere a value must be unpredictable.
Check whether nonces are guaranteed unique or merely random, and prefer uniqueness.
Look for a fork, restore or snapshot path that could reproduce generator state.
defensive: Use the operating system or a vetted library for every security-relevant random value.
Prefer counters or explicit uniqueness guarantees for nonces where the construction allows it.
Reseed appropriately after virtual machine snapshot or restore operations.
Treat any code that rolls its own random generator as unsafe until proven otherwise.
Use constant-time comparisons for values compared against attacker input, since a timing difference leaks information.

topics.name: Common Crypto Failures and How They Become Real
topics.description: The recurring classes of cryptographic failure — obsolete primitives, missing authentication, downgrades and implementation bugs — and how each one turns into an incident.

content.overview: Cryptographic code fails in recurring ways, and the failures are rarely in the mathematics. They are in the choices around it: what is encrypted, what is verified, and what is compared.
how_it_works: Encrypting without authenticating lets an attacker modify the ciphertext, so a decryption failure must stop the application rather than be ignored.
Comparing values with an ordinary string comparison can leak the correct value through timing, so secret comparisons must be constant time.
Padding oracles let an attacker learn about plaintext from error behaviour, which is why modern schemes avoid them or make errors indistinguishable.
Inventing a construction from sound primitives can still be insecure, because a scheme is more than the sum of its parts.
Failing open on an error, such as accepting traffic when verification is unavailable, turns a security control into an availability preference.
history: Early application code decrypted and then trusted the result, so errors were informative by default.
A long series of padding oracle vulnerabilities demonstrated that error handling alone can break an otherwise sound scheme.
High-level libraries absorbed many of these lessons, and the residual failures are now mostly in how applications use them.
Framework guidance now forbids rolling your own crypto in most languages for exactly this reason.
real_world: A verification error that is logged and then ignored lets an attacker tamper with signed data without anyone noticing.
A timing side channel on a token comparison is difficult to notice and difficult to fix once shipped.
Using a fast hash for signatures with a short key length reduces the scheme to something that can be brute forced.
what_to_look_for: Confirm every message is verified before it is trusted, and that verification failure stops processing.
Look for ordinary equality comparisons on anything secret, including tokens and session identifiers.
Check that error paths fail closed rather than falling back to an allowed state.
Check algorithm and key length choices against current guidance rather than against what the library defaults to years ago.
defensive: Authenticate before you act on data, and treat any verification error as fatal.
Use constant-time comparison functions provided by the platform rather than writing your own.
Never invent a construction; choose a named, reviewed one and use it as documented.
Keep libraries updated, because most crypto failures live in code that has not been revised.
Have cryptographic choices reviewed by someone who did not write the feature.

topics.name: Key Management: Generate, Store, Rotate, Revoke
topics.description: Where cryptography meets operations: generating keys from real randomness, storing them away from the data, rotating on a schedule, and revoking before you are forced to.

content.overview: Most organisations can deploy strong cryptography and still lose data because the keys are poorly managed. The algorithm is rarely the weak point; storage, rotation and revocation are.
how_it_works: Keys are generated with a good random source, then stored somewhere with tighter access than the data they protect.
Separate keys per purpose and per environment, so a test key can never be used against production data.
Rotation limits how much traffic or data a single key can expose, and rotation only helps if it actually happens.
Revocation says a key must never be used again, which requires something that checks rather than something that logs.
A key management system should record who used which key for what, because that is what an investigation needs.
history: Keys were once kept in application configuration, which meant they appeared in source control and in every copy of the system.
Hardware security modules gave a place to keep keys that code could use but could not read.
Cloud secret managers made managed keys broadly available, but also created a central point of failure worth attacking.
Managed key management with automatic rotation became the default expectation, which makes manual key handling the outlier.
real_world: A key committed to a source repository may still be live years later, and history makes deleting the file irrelevant.
One key reused across every environment means a single test-system compromise can affect production data.
A key that is rotated but never retired leaves the old one usable, so the rotation provides no benefit at all.
what_to_look_for: Check whether keys appear in source control, build logs, container images or client-side code.
Confirm development, test and production use different keys.
Check whether retired keys are actually destroyed, and whether that is verified rather than assumed.
Check who can read keys, and whether that access is logged.
defensive: Store keys in a managed secret store or hardware module, never in application code or configuration files.
Use separate keys per environment and per purpose, and label them so misuse is obvious.
Automate rotation, and verify that old material is destroyed afterwards.
Give key access its own access reviews, since it is more sensitive than the data itself.
Scan source history and build artefacts for secrets, because removing them later does not remove them.
Rehearse revocation, since a key you cannot revoke is really a key you cannot rotate.

topics.name: How an OS Is Organised: Kernel, Users, Files, Permissions
topics.description: Inside every operating system: what the kernel does, why user and kernel mode exist, how a program asks for a file, and where identity and permissions enter the request.

content.overview: An operating system is the layer that owns the hardware and decides who gets to use it. Almost every security boundary you rely on is a decision this layer makes on your behalf.
how_it_works: The kernel runs with full privilege and is the only component that talks directly to hardware.
Everything above it, including every application, runs as an unprivileged process with restricted access.
A user account and a process identity are separate, but both are checked before privileged operations are allowed.
The filesystem stores data and metadata together, so ownership and permissions travel with the file itself.
Memory is allocated in separated regions per process, and the enforcement of that separation is the core of process isolation.
history: Batch systems gave one user the whole machine, so the operating system was mainly a scheduler.
Timesharing and then personal computing introduced the need to separate users from each other.
The Unix permission model became the basis for a portable approach to file and process security that Windows also partly adopted.
Hardware support for virtualisation made it practical to run whole operating systems isolated from one another.
real_world: A service running as root has no meaningful boundary, so a flaw in it is effectively a flaw in the whole system.
A file copied to another user still carries its original owner and mode, which is why copied files can become more or less exposed.
A crash in one process should not affect another, and when it does the isolation model is not doing its job.
what_to_look_for: Check which user each critical service runs as, and whether that is the least privileged option that works.
Check the permissions on files holding credentials, configuration and keys.
Notice setuid and setgid bits, which change the effective user of a program and deserve explicit review.
Check whether sensitive data is separated from unprivileged users in memory as well as on disk.
defensive: Run each service under its own dedicated, unprivileged account.
Grant the minimum permissions needed and review anything with elevated file attributes.
Separate sensitive data with operating system controls rather than relying on application logic.
Patch the operating system itself, since kernel flaws undermine every isolation guarantee above it.

topics.name: Windows Security Model: Tokens, UAC and Active Directory Basics
topics.description: How Windows decides what you may do: access tokens, what User Account Control changes about them, and why directory accounts multiply the blast radius of a single mistake.

content.overview: Windows security is built around access tokens, integrity levels and objects that list who may do what. Most Windows privilege escalation is a mismatch between those and how an application actually uses them.
how_it_works: Every logged-in session has an access token describing the user, their groups and their privileges.
Access checks compare that token against the access control list on each object, so the same user has different access to different objects.
Integrity levels add a second dimension, separating what an ordinary process may read from what a service may write.
User Account Control runs most of the desktop as a filtered standard-user token and only elevates specific operations.
Active Directory extends the same model to identities across a network, which is why a local account problem can become a domain one.
history: Windows NT replaced the older Windows with an explicit security model, including objects, tokens and descriptors.
User Account Control arrived because the standard user and administrator split was routinely undermined by applications requesting elevation constantly.
Active Directory and Group Policy turned Windows identity into the standard way large organisations manage access.
Later integrity levels, mandatory integrity control and virtualization-based security narrowed the paths from a compromised process to the system.
real_world: An application configured to run with full administrator rights loses every boundary the operating system would otherwise provide.
A service account with domain administrator rights turns one application flaw into a domain compromise.
A stored credential on a machine can be extracted and replayed, which is why the operating system tries to limit where it can be used.
what_to_look_for: Check whether any application is configured to run as administrator, and remove it if it can run without.
Check which accounts are in the local administrators group, since membership is persistent across restarts.
Notice stored credentials and machine account passwords, which are high-value targets.
Check that privileged actions require elevation rather than being silently performed.
defensive: Run day-to-day work as a standard user and elevate only for specific, visible operations.
Use separate, least-privileged service accounts rather than reusing an administrator account.
Restrict who can join local administrators and review that membership regularly.
Enable credential protection features your version supports, so stored secrets are harder to extract.
Treat any single point of failure account in the administrators group as a priority for review.

topics.name: Linux Permissions, Users and Groups
topics.description: Read and reason about Linux permissions: owner, group and other bits, octal and symbolic modes, and why setuid, the sticky bit and shared accounts decide who can change what.

content.overview: Linux file permissions and ownership are simple enough to reason about in full. That simplicity is the point: a reviewer can usually tell whether an access decision is correct just by looking.
how_it_works: Every file has an owner, a group and a set of permission bits for the owner, the group and everyone else.
Directory permissions mean something different from file permissions: read lists names, write creates or deletes entries, and search permits traversal.
Processes run with a user and a group, and may temporarily gain additional groups.
Special permissions such as setuid and setgid change the effective identity used for access decisions.
Access is decided on the path, so a directory without search permission blocks access to everything beneath it.
history: The Unix permission model was designed to be understandable, with three classes and three bits rather than a growing access control list.
Access control lists and mandatory access control were later added for cases the simple model could not express.
Container platforms rely heavily on user namespaces and capabilities, which extend the model rather than replace it.
Modern distros ship with additional confinement features because the simple model has known gaps.
real_world: A world-readable private key file is one of the most common and most avoidable exposures on a Linux server.
A service running as root does not benefit from any file permission restriction, so a single flaw has full effect.
A directory with write permission for a group lets any member rename or delete files beneath it, regardless of the file own permissions.
what_to_look_for: Look for world-readable files that should be restricted, especially keys and configuration with secrets.
Check which user each service runs as, and whether it has the privileges it actually needs.
Review setuid and setgid bits, since they change effective identity silently.
Check directory permissions, because they can grant or remove access regardless of the files inside.
defensive: Restrict sensitive files to their owning user, and verify with an unprivileged account rather than by eye.
Run services as dedicated unprivileged users, and use capabilities for specific privileges instead of running as root.
Review setuid and setgid entries, and remove any that are not clearly required.
Use directories to apply default permissions to new files, so correct access is inherited rather than remembered.
Audit with a listing of ownership and mode rather than trusting the intentions of whoever created the file.

topics.name: The Command Line for Security Work
topics.description: Work in a shell on purpose: how commands, pipes and redirection compose, which commands answer security questions, and which ones can quietly destroy data.

content.overview: The command line is where security work becomes precise. It is also where mistakes have immediate effect, so the same power that makes it useful makes it worth treating carefully.
how_it_works: Commands read arguments and options, and the shell interprets quoting, expansion and redirection before anything runs.
Privilege is inherited, so a command run as root affects the system and not just a user session.
A pipeline passes output from one command to another, which is fast to write and hard to read later.
History and shell logging record what was typed, so a secret passed on the command line can persist on disk.
Scripting multiplies whatever habits you have, including the habits of skipping verification.
history: Unix treated small composable tools as the primary interface, which is why its tooling is scriptable by default.
Windows gained a capable command shell but most system administration still happened through a graphical console.
Container and orchestration tooling moved much of operations back to the command line out of necessity.
Remote execution tools now make it routine to run administrative commands across many machines, which raises the cost of a mistake.
real_world: A destructive command with a wildcard can remove far more than intended, and shell completion makes the wrong path easier to select.
A password typed as a command argument appears in shell history, in process listings and in any command log.
Piping output into a shell that interprets it turns a data source into a way to execute commands.
what_to_look_for: Prefer running a command that reports what it will do before one that changes anything.
Check whether a destructive command has a dry-run or confirmation option, and use it.
Avoid passing secrets on the command line, and use an input mechanism that does not record them.
Re-read any command you are about to run as an administrator, since the blast radius is the whole system.
defensive: Use the least privileged account that can complete the task, and escalate only for the specific step that needs it.
Pass secrets through standard input or a file with tight permissions, not as arguments.
Read scripts before running them, and treat a script from the internet as unreviewed code.
Keep a written record of administrative commands, because the shell history is not an audit log.
Use version control for configuration changes so a mistake is reversible.

topics.name: Processes, Services and Persistence Mechanisms
topics.description: What a running program actually is, how services start and survive a reboot, and the operating-system features that keep code alive — plus where each one leaves evidence.

content.overview: A running program is a process, and a process that should survive a reboot is usually a service. Attackers establish persistence here, so understanding how things start is how you find what should not be running.
how_it_works: A process has a parent, a user, open files and network connections, and all of that is visible to an administrator.
A service is a process the operating system starts automatically and restarts when it exits.
Persistence is usually a scheduled task, a startup folder entry, a new service registration or a modified startup script.
The order in which the system starts these things defines a race, and attackers often aim to win it.
Every persistence mechanism leaves a record in a specific place, which is why enumerating those places is high value.
history: Manual startup scripts were the original persistence mechanism and are still widely used and widely abused.
The Windows registry became a convenient hiding place, and remains one of the most common.
Scheduled tasks added reliable recurring execution, and became a standard offensive technique.
Modern endpoint tooling watches these locations continuously, which raised the bar for staying hidden.
real_world: A service running from a user profile directory rather than a system path is unusual and worth investigating.
A scheduled task that runs a script from a temporary location is a common persistence mechanism after an initial compromise.
A process with no parent, or with a parent that has already exited, suggests it was started in an unusual way.
what_to_look_for: Enumerate services, scheduled tasks and startup entries on a regular schedule and compare against a known baseline.
Check what account each service runs as and what it executes.
Notice binaries running from temporary, download or user-writable directories.
Look for processes with no parent process, which can indicate injection or manual start.
defensive: Baseline services, scheduled tasks and startup entries, and alert on changes.
Restrict who can create or modify services and scheduled tasks, since both are privileged operations.
Keep administrative tooling and temporary directories out of the search path for services.
Prefer a service account with no interactive logon, so a compromised service cannot be used to log in.
Investigate unsigned or unexpectedly named binaries that start automatically.

topics.name: Logs: Where the OS Tells You What Happened
topics.description: What Windows and Linux record, what a useful event actually contains, why logs must leave the machine they describe, and how raw records become an alert someone can act on.

content.overview: The operating system records what happened. If nobody collects, keeps and reads those records, an incident investigation is limited to whatever a user reports.
how_it_works: Each platform has its own event log format and its own idea of what is worth recording by default.
Default logging usually records failures well and successes poorly, which is a problem when investigating misuse.
Authentication events are the most commonly needed, and are also the most commonly not recorded completely.
Logs are only useful if they survive the attack, so they belong somewhere an administrator cannot casually delete them.
Time matters: if clocks disagree, correlating records from different systems becomes guesswork.
history: Event logging on personal systems was minimal and locally controlled by the user.
Organisations adopted central logging mainly to satisfy audits rather than to detect attacks.
The realisation that an attacker with local administrator access can usually clear local logs drove adoption of centralised collection.
Detection engineering later shifted the goal from storing logs to using them to generate useful alerts.
real_world: A ransomware incident becomes far easier to scope when authentication logs survived and were sent off the host.
A single failed login three years after the fact is the only evidence of an intrusion that was never detected.
A system whose clock drifted produces an audit trail that appears internally consistent and is entirely wrong.
what_to_look_for: Check which event categories are recorded, and whether successful logins are included as well as failures.
Check where logs are stored and whether a local administrator can delete them.
Check clock synchronisation across systems whose records you intend to correlate.
Check the retention period, and whether it matches the time an investigation might realistically take.
defensive: Centralise log collection so an attacker with host access cannot erase the record.
Enable logging for administrative actions, privilege changes and successful authentications.
Synchronise time across systems, because unsynchronised logs cannot be correlated reliably.
Set retention to match or exceed the longest realistic investigation window.
Alert on the events that indicate a problem, because an unread log is an archive rather than a control.

topics.name: Patching, Updates and Vulnerability Management
topics.description: Why patching is a programme rather than a click: knowing what you run, prioritising by exposure and evidence of use, deploying safely, and proving the fix actually landed.

content.overview: Patching closes known weaknesses. What matters is not the volume of updates applied but whether the ones that matter reached the systems that are actually exposed.
how_it_works: A vulnerability has a severity rating and a known fix, and both depend on context you have to supply.
Prioritisation should weigh exposure and what the weakness allows, not just the published score.
A system that cannot be patched can often be mitigated by configuration, segmentation or monitoring instead.
Applications and their dependencies are usually a larger source of risk than the operating system itself.
A patch process that can be bypassed quietly is not a patch process, and this is where attackers actually work.
history: Patching was a periodic, largely manual activity tied to operating system releases.
Attackers standardised on exploiting the gap between disclosure and deployment, and that gap still drives most intrusion.
Software composition analysis brought third-party components into scope, which sharply increased the visible volume of findings.
Modern approaches attempt to make patches hard to bypass, treating the update channel itself as privileged infrastructure.
real_world: An internet-facing system missing a critical update is the most common finding in external assessments.
A build pipeline that lets a developer bypass the security step makes every policy a suggestion.
A component that is no longer maintained will never receive a fix, so something else has to compensate.
what_to_look_for: Know your inventory first, since you cannot patch a system you do not know exists.
Check which systems are internet-reachable and compare that against their patch level.
Check third-party and open-source dependencies, which are frequently older than the application code.
Check whether the update path itself requires an account with administrative rights, since that is where bypasses happen.
defensive: Prioritise by exposure and impact, and record the reasoning for anything deferred.
Patch internet-facing systems on a short timescale and internal systems on a longer one.
Remove software that is unmaintained rather than hoping it stays safe.
Restrict and monitor the update channel so it cannot be bypassed quietly.
Rebuild from known-good images periodically, since long-lived machines drift from their original state.

topics.name: Endpoint Protection: AV, EDR and Application Control
topics.description: What signature scanning actually checks, what endpoint detection adds over the top of it, and why controlling which software may run beats hoping detection notices.

content.overview: Endpoint protection has moved from scanning for known bad files to watching behaviour. The change is significant: detection now depends on what a process does, not only what it is called.
how_it_works: Antivirus compares files against known-bad signatures and reputation, which works well for known threats.
Behavioural detection watches a process tree and its actions, and can flag a novel program doing something suspicious.
Endpoint detection and response additionally records activity centrally, so an investigation is not limited to one machine.
Application control allows only approved programs to run, which removes whole categories of risk at the cost of flexibility.
Cloud-delivered lookup improves detection latency, which is why a machine that has been offline is a blind spot.
history: Signature-based antivirus dominated for two decades and worked well against the threat model it was built for.
Polymorphic and packed malware defeated signatures, and heuristics were added to compensate.
Fileless techniques, which run entirely in memory, broke file scanning almost entirely and drove behavioural approaches.
Managed detection and response added human analysts on top of telemetry, because tooling alone does not keep up.
real_world: A system with endpoint protection disabled is often disabled to make a specific application work, which removes the control permanently.
Allow-listing one folder for an installer can become a permanent gap in a policy that was meant to be temporary.
A detection that fires constantly and is always ignored teaches everyone to ignore it, which is worse than not having it.
what_to_look_for: Check whether endpoint protection is actually running and reporting, not merely installed.
Check for exclusions, since each one is a deliberate hole in the control.
Check whether telemetry is reaching the central system, since local-only logs are lost if the host is reimaged.
Check how many alerts are open and how long they have been open.
defensive: Keep endpoint protection enabled and reporting centrally, and treat disabling it as an exception with an expiry date.
Minimise exclusions, and document why each is needed.
Enable behavioural detection and application control where the environment supports it.
Tune alerts so the ones that matter are not buried, and measure how long a real alert takes to be actioned.
Keep definitions and platform current, since old signatures protect against old threats only.

topics.name: Hardening a Fresh Install (CIS-style Baselines)
topics.description: Turn a default install into a defensible system: what a security baseline contains, how to apply one safely, how to verify it, and how to keep it true as the system changes.

content.overview: Hardening a new system means removing what you do not need, restricting what remains, and turning on the logging that tells you what happens later. The order matters, because each step reduces the next.
how_it_works: Start from a documented baseline rather than from defaults, so the result is reproducible and reviewable.
Remove unnecessary software, accounts and services, because every one of them is a future maintenance and attack obligation.
Restrict administrative access to named accounts, and remove shared or default ones.
Turn on the logging and monitoring that you will want during an incident, before you need it.
Apply configuration as code so the baseline can be rebuilt and compared, rather than drifting machine by machine.
history: Early hardening was a checklist applied once to individual machines, with no way to verify it stayed applied.
Configuration management made baselines repeatable, and compliance frameworks provided the specific settings to apply.
Cloud platforms shifted part of the control from the machine to the platform, changing what a baseline even means.
Current practice treats a hardened image as a build artifact that is rebuilt regularly rather than a machine that is patched indefinitely.
real_world: A default administrator account with a known password left enabled is still one of the most common serious findings.
A server that does not need to be on the internet should not be, and removing that requirement removes a whole class of exposure.
A hardened baseline applied once and never verified gives false confidence, because configuration drift is continuous.
what_to_look_for: Check which accounts can administer the system and whether each one is still needed.
Check which services are running and whether the software is still supported.
Check whether the documented baseline actually matches what is deployed.
Check that logging and time synchronisation are enabled before an incident, not during one.
defensive: Define a documented baseline and enforce it automatically rather than by hand.
Remove default accounts, sample applications and unused network listeners.
Require multi-factor authentication for every administrative path, including ones only reachable internally.
Enable logging for authentication, privilege changes and administrative actions from the start.
Rebuild machines from hardened images periodically, so drift is corrected by replacing rather than by patching.

topics.name: Accounts, Identifiers and Why Identity Is the New Perimeter
topics.description: What an account really is, how identifiers differ from credentials and sessions, and why attackers now log in instead of breaking in.

content.overview: Identity is the security boundary that actually matters today. Almost nothing is reachable because of where it sits on a network; it is reachable because of who is asking.
how_it_works: An account is a set of credentials, an identity is what that account represents, and the difference matters for revocation.
Authentication establishes who is asking. Authorisation then decides what that identity may do.
Machine and human identities behave differently: one is consumed by software, the other by a person who can be phished.
Group membership is the usual way permissions are granted, so a single group change can grant a lot at once.
Because access is evaluated per request, the same identity may have different reach at different times.
history: Networks were originally trusted by location, so a machine on the internal network was implicitly an authorised user.
As users became remote, identity became the boundary and directory services became the place where it is defined.
Single sign-on reduced the number of passwords to remember and concentrated the risk in the identity provider.
Cloud platforms added short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials in place of long-lived shared secrets.
real_world: A service account with far more access than the application needs turns an application flaw into a broad compromise.
A contractor who keeps access after a project ends is one of the most common access-review findings.
An account that can reach production because it sits in a convenience group is an access problem that looks like a network problem.
what_to_look_for: List every identity with administrative or production access, and check each one still needs it.
Check which permissions arrive by group membership rather than by an explicit grant.
Notice machine identities, since they are rarely reviewed and rarely expire.
Check whether an identity is used interactively by a person as well as by software, which complicates attribution.
defensive: Create a distinct identity per person and per workload, and never share one.
Grant the minimum access each identity needs, and review group membership regularly.
Prefer short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials for workloads over permanent shared keys.
Remove access automatically when someone leaves or changes role.
Log identity use, so you can tell a person from a service after the fact.

topics.name: Passwords: Creation, Storage and Rotation Reality
topics.description: What identity guidance actually says about password length, composition rules and forced changes — and why the reset flow is the real attack surface.

content.overview: Everything about passwords has changed except the advice most people still receive. Length and uniqueness matter far more than symbol substitutions, and storage matters more than creation rules.
how_it_works: A password is a shared secret, so its strength is entirely a function of how unpredictable it is to an attacker.
Human-chosen passwords cluster around predictable patterns, which is why length beats complexity rules.
A breach of one service makes every reused password vulnerable everywhere, and reuse is common.
Storage decides how much a leak costs: a memory-hard salted hash makes guessing expensive per attempt.
Rotation was widely recommended, but forced frequent rotation often produces weaker passwords and is now discouraged without evidence of compromise.
history: Password-only authentication dominated, with complexity rules enforced by systems rather than chosen by users.
Breach corpora made reuse attacks practical, and check-your-breach services turned the problem into a checklist.
Password managers removed the cognitive cost of long unique passwords and changed what good practice looks like.
Passkeys and multi-factor authentication have started to remove the password as the primary factor entirely.
real_world: A leaked database stored with a fast hash is cracked quickly, and rotating afterward does not help users who reused the password.
A policy demanding a symbol and a digit at eight characters produces predictable patterns that fall quickly to guessing.
Shared team passwords are rarely rotated, and are frequently the weakest credential in the environment.
what_to_look_for: Check the storage algorithm, the salt and the work factor, since those decide what a leak costs.
Check the length and uniqueness policy, and whether it pushes people toward predictable patterns.
Check whether rotation is enforced on a schedule rather than in response to evidence.
Check that shared accounts are identified, since they defeat attribution and revocation.
defensive: Store passwords with a memory-hard function, a unique salt and a tuned work factor.
Encourage long, unique, generated passwords through a manager rather than mandating symbol rules.
Check new and changed passwords against known breached lists.
Stop forcing periodic rotation unless there is evidence of compromise, and require rotation on any suspected exposure.
Eliminate shared passwords entirely by giving each person and workload its own identity.

topics.name: Multi-Factor Authentication and Passkeys
topics.description: How a second factor really changes the cost of account takeover, why SMS and passkeys are not equivalent, and the attacks that still beat weaker factors.

content.overview: Multi-factor authentication is the single most effective control available to most organisations, and passkeys are the version that finally works without users fighting it.
how_it_works: A factor is something you know, something you have, or something you are, and using two of the three is what makes it strong.
One-time codes are widely deployed and much better than nothing, but they are phishable and can be relayed.
Push approvals are better, but an approval prompt that does not describe the request is easy to accept by reflex.
Passkeys use a public and private key pair, so the site never sees a secret that can be replayed.
Because the private key stays on the device, a passkey resists phishing by construction rather than by user vigilance.
history: One-time passcodes were introduced as a simple second factor and remain the most common implementation.
Push-based approval arrived to fix the code-phishing problem but introduced approval-fatigue instead.
Passkeys were standardised by the industry and are now supported by the major platform and browser vendors.
Syncing passkeys across a user account made them practical for people who lose devices and change phones.
real_world: An attacker who asks an employee to approve a push notification can take over the account in one call.
Number matching reduces the usefulness of a phishing page because the attacker does not know the code in advance.
A passkey on a synced account is still far safer than a password, and much safer than an SMS code.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the second factor is phishable, such as a code or an uncontextualised push approval.
Check that multi-factor is required rather than merely available.
Check how recovery works, since a weak recovery path bypasses the factor entirely.
Check that administrative and remote access require a factor, not only ordinary sign-in.
defensive: Require multi-factor authentication everywhere, starting with email and administrative access.
Prefer passkeys, then number-matched codes, and treat SMS as a last resort.
Make approval prompts describe the specific request and origin, so a blind approval is a mistake.
Harden account recovery as carefully as sign-in, since attackers go to the easier door.
Remove the option to disable the factor for an account, and alert on any attempt to.

topics.name: Session Management and Account Takeover
topics.description: Session tokens, cookies and timeouts explained by mechanism: session fixation, session hijacking, and why a stolen session is not the same risk as a stolen password.

content.overview: A session is proof that somebody authenticated, carried in a token. How that token is created, stored, scoped and invalidated determines whether an attacker who steals it gains much.
how_it_works: A login creates a session identifier, and from then on the token stands in for the credential.
An identifier in a cookie is convenient for the application and convenient for an attacker who can read the cookie.
Binding the session to something the attacker does not have, such as a device key, removes the value of a stolen token.
Session lifetime is a direct trade-off: longer sessions are friendlier and give an attacker more time.
Invalidating a session on logout, password change and privilege change is what makes revocation meaningful.
history: Sessions were originally server-side state referenced by an identifier, which meant the identifier was the whole security story.
Stateless approaches moved the state into a signed token, which is efficient but makes revocation harder.
Session fixation and hijacking were the dominant web vulnerabilities for years and drove most of the current cookie guidance.
Device binding and passkeys reduce the value of a stolen token rather than only shortening its life.
real_world: A session identifier that never changes after login can be fixed by an attacker before the victim signs in.
A session token stored where page scripts can read it is exposed to any cross-site scripting flaw.
Logging out that only clears a cookie on the client leaves a still-valid token in the hands of anyone who copied it.
what_to_look_for: Check that the session identifier changes on login, which prevents session fixation.
Check the cookie flags, especially secure, HttpOnly and an appropriate SameSite value.
Check session lifetime and whether idle sessions expire.
Check that logout and password change actually invalidate the session server-side.
defensive: Regenerate the session identifier on every privilege change, especially at login.
Set secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on session cookies, and keep the lifetime short.
Invalidate sessions server-side on logout, password change and suspected compromise.
Bind sessions to a device key where possible, so a stolen token alone is not enough.
Provide a way to see and revoke active sessions, so a lost device is recoverable.

topics.name: Authorisation vs Authentication: Least Privilege in Practice
topics.description: Why 'who are you' and 'what may you do' have to be answered separately — deny by default, least privilege, and the failures that leave signed-in users over-privileged.

content.overview: Authentication and authorisation are different questions, and most serious application breaches are authorisation failures rather than authentication ones. Broken access control has ranked first in the most recent industry survey for exactly this reason.
how_it_works: Authentication asks who this is. Authorisation asks whether this identity may perform this action on this resource.
The correct authorisation decision needs the identity, the action and the specific object, not just the route.
Default-deny means a request is rejected unless a rule explicitly allows it, which is the safer default.
Least privilege means each identity receives only the access its task requires, and no more.
Enforcement belongs on the server for every request, because the client is under the user control.
history: Early applications checked authentication in the interface and assumed that was sufficient.
As APIs grew, authorisation moved to the server, but was often implemented per endpoint, which led to inconsistent rules.
The industry survey began ranking broken access control as a leading category, which changed what teams prioritised.
Centralised policy engines emerged so authorisation decisions could be written once and applied consistently.
real_world: Hiding a delete button in the interface leaves the endpoint available, and the request can be sent directly.
A record identifier in a request is often treated as proof of permission, which lets one user reach another data.
An endpoint that checks only that a user is logged in, and not which records belong to them, is a very common flaw.
what_to_look_for: Check whether every endpoint that touches a specific object verifies permission for that object.
Check for authorisation enforced only in the client, which is not enforcement.
Check whether a role can be supplied by the user, since a client-supplied role is not a decision.
Check that denied requests are logged, because silent denial is how these flaws persist.
defensive: Default to deny and grant explicitly, so a forgotten rule fails safely.
Check permission on the object being acted on, not only on the route being called.
Keep authorisation decisions on the server and repeat them on every request.
Centralise policy so endpoints cannot quietly implement contradictory rules.
Test with two accounts of different privilege, which finds these flaws faster than any scanner.

topics.name: Directory Services, SSO and Federation
topics.description: Where entitlements really come from: directories as the source of truth, what single sign-on concentrates, and how a signed identity assertion crosses an organisation boundary.

content.overview: A directory service is the single place identities and their relationships are defined. Single sign-on and federation let one authenticated identity reach many systems, which is convenient and concentrates risk.
how_it_works: The directory stores identities, their attributes and their group memberships.
Authentication is usually delegated to a single provider, and other systems accept its assertion of identity.
Federation extends that across organisational boundaries, so a partner identity can be accepted under agreed conditions.
Claims carry what the provider asserts, and trusting too much in a claim is how access leaks across boundaries.
Group membership decided in the directory becomes access everywhere, which makes the directory a high-value target.
history: Directories existed to manage users and resources, and became identity stores once authentication moved into them.
Single sign-on was adopted to reduce password prompts, and the resulting dependency became a concentration of risk.
Federation protocols standardised cross-organisational trust, which also made misconfiguration more consequential.
Modern approaches increasingly use short-lived, audience-restricted tokens so a stolen assertion is limited.
real_world: A directory compromise is worse than a single application compromise, because it affects everything that trusts it.
A group that includes both staff and service identities can grant a human the permissions intended for a program.
An application that accepts a token without checking the intended audience will accept tokens meant for another service.
what_to_look_for: Check which systems trust the directory, since that is the blast radius of a directory compromise.
Check that tokens are audience-restricted, and that the receiving system verifies it.
Check group membership, since it is where most access is actually granted.
Check the lifetime of issued tokens and whether they can be revoked.
defensive: Protect the directory as tier-zero infrastructure, with strong authentication and tight administrative access.
Restrict every application trust to the specific directory and services it needs.
Issue short-lived, audience-restricted tokens, and verify the audience on receipt.
Review group membership on a schedule, and remove identities that no longer need access.
Require multi-factor authentication on the directory itself, ahead of any other system.

topics.name: Privilege Escalation and Admin Account Hygiene
topics.description: How a routine account gains rights it was never granted, why standing admin access is the real problem, and the hygiene that keeps elevation rare.

content.overview: Privilege escalation turns a limited foothold into control of the system. Most of it succeeds because of ordinary configuration mistakes rather than clever exploitation.
how_it_works: Escalation means moving from one level of access to a higher one, either by exploiting a flaw or by abusing a permissive setting.
Misconfigured service permissions, over-broad file permissions and unattended administrative sessions are the usual route.
Scheduled tasks and services are frequently configured to run with more privilege than the work requires.
Administrator accounts used for daily work turn any credential theft into full control immediately.
Separating a standard account from an administrative one makes this class of escalation much harder.
history: Local privilege escalation was largely about predictable service paths and permissive file permissions.
Kernel and driver exploits were the high-profile route, and are still the route when configuration is sound.
Token and impersonation features gave applications ways to act as other users, which is powerful and frequently misconfigured.
Current guidance is dominated by removing the permissions that made escalation possible in the first place.
real_world: A service that can read a file only administrators should read is a complete escalation path on its own.
An unquoted service path lets an attacker place an executable earlier in the search order and run it as the service.
A single administrative account for an entire team means one stolen laptop is a domain compromise.
what_to_look_for: Check service and task permissions, since these are the most common local escalation path.
Check whether the administrative accounts used day to day are separate from standard user accounts.
Check file permissions on program directories and configuration files.
Check how many accounts are administrators, since more than a handful is a finding in itself.
defensive: Run day-to-day work as a standard user and elevate only for specific tasks.
Give services the minimum privilege they need, and check their file and directory permissions.
Use absolute or quoted paths in service definitions so an attacker cannot substitute a binary.
Give each administrator a separate named account, and use just-in-time elevation where available.
Monitor for new members of privileged groups, which is the event that precedes most escalation chains.

topics.name: Service Accounts, API Keys and Secrets Management
topics.description: Machine identities outnumber people in most systems: how a hard-coded API key becomes a permanent back door, and what replaces long-lived shared secrets.

content.overview: Machine identities outnumber human ones and are reviewed far less often. A leaked service credential is often a long-lived key that grants broad access and is invisible in account review.
how_it_works: A service account is a real account used by software, so it can log in interactively unless you prevent it.
An API key is a shared secret, and anyone holding it inherits every permission it was granted.
A stored credential such as a certificate or a managed identity removes the shared secret entirely.
Rotation is difficult for embedded credentials, which is why so many of them are permanent.
Scope is the main defence: a narrowly scoped, short-lived credential limits the damage even if it leaks.
history: Software integrations were built by copying a password into a configuration file, which is still a common pattern.
Infrastructure as code brought managed identities, so a workload could be given an identity without storing a secret.
Secrets management products made rotation routine, and made secret sprawl visible for the first time.
Workload identity federation extended the same idea to external and third-party workloads.
real_world: An API key with administrator rights, committed to a repository, is a complete compromise that is often still live years later.
A service account permitted to log in interactively gives an attacker a persistent administrative identity.
A credential rotated in the secret store but still hard-coded in an application gains nothing, because the old copy still works.
what_to_look_for: Check where credentials are stored, and whether any appear in source control, images or client-side code.
Check what permission each service identity holds, and whether it matches the work it does.
Check whether service accounts can log in interactively.
Check whether rotation actually reaches every copy of the credential in use.
defensive: Prefer a workload identity over a stored secret wherever the platform offers one.
Scope every service identity to the smallest set of permissions the work needs.
Disable interactive logon for service accounts, so a stolen credential cannot be used by a person.
Scan source history and build artefacts for secrets, since removing a file later does not remove the secret.
Automate rotation and verify that old credentials stop working, rather than assuming it.

topics.name: Access Reviews, Joiner–Mover–Leaver and Deprovisioning
topics.description: Access accumulates unless something removes it: how joiner–mover–leaver processes, recertification and timely deprovisioning keep identities honest.

content.overview: Most over-privileged accounts are not created maliciously. They accumulate because nobody removes access when a person or a project changes, and that accumulation is the actual vulnerability.
how_it_works: A joiner needs access, a mover needs different access, and a leaver needs none at all.
Access is usually granted to a person directly, so each new role creates another grant rather than a replacement.
A review is only useful if it forces removal, not just confirmation that the list looks right.
Group-based access reduces the number of individual decisions but can hide who actually has access.
Deprovisioning has to be triggered by something reliable, or it becomes a manual process that will eventually be missed.
history: Access was managed by hand, so reviews were rare and sampled, and errors accumulated silently.
Identity governance tooling made it possible to see who has access to what across many systems.
Certification campaigns introduced a periodic, deliberate approval step, which removed a great deal of unnecessary access.
Automated joiner-mover-leaver flows reduced the delay between a role change and the access change that should follow it.
real_world: An employee who changed role three years ago still has their old administrative rights on a system nobody remembers.
A contractor keeps access to a project system long after the project closed, and nobody owns the system to remove it.
A review where the reviewer approves everything within a minute changes nothing at all.
what_to_look_for: Check how long high-privilege access has existed without being reviewed, and whether reviews happen at all.
Compare current access against the person actual current role, not their original one.
Check whether leaver removal is automatic or manual, and how long it takes.
Check whether a group has grown over time without anyone examining what it now grants.
defensive: Trigger joiner, mover and leaver actions from the human resources system rather than from memory.
Review privileged access on a schedule, and require the reviewer to actively remove what is not justified.
Make removals faster than grants, since a missed removal is the more common and more damaging error.
Base access on groups with a clear business owner, so a review has something specific to examine.
Report unused entitlements, because access nobody needs is the easiest thing to remove.

topics.name: Data Classification: What You Actually Need to Protect
topics.description: How to sort information into protection tiers, write a handling rule for each one, and avoid the twin failures of classifying nothing and classifying everything.

content.overview: Data classification is the step that decides what protection something deserves. Without it, every item is treated the same way, which usually means the sensitive items are not protected enough.
how_it_works: Classification assigns a level based on sensitivity and the harm disclosure would cause.
Each level maps to controls: where the data may be stored, who may see it, how it is encrypted, and how long it is kept.
Classification is only useful if the mapping to controls is written down and enforced by systems.
The hardest part is usually deciding the level for new data, and getting people to label it consistently.
Retention is part of classification, because data nobody needs should not exist at all.
history: Physical filing systems used clear markings like confidential, which translated directly once data became digital.
Regulatory definitions introduced formal categories tied to specific legal obligations rather than to intuition.
Cloud storage made it technically easy to apply different controls per classification, which turned policy into configuration.
Data discovery tooling emerged because nobody actually knew where all the sensitive data lived.
real_world: A spreadsheet of customer records in a general-purpose shared folder is the most common classification failure in practice.
Data that is correctly classified but stored without encryption loses its protection the moment storage is misconfigured.
Labeling that depends on the user judgement produces wildly inconsistent results across a large organisation.
what_to_look_for: Check whether a written classification scheme exists and whether the levels map to specific controls.
Check where the most sensitive data actually lives, rather than where policy says it should.
Check whether retention periods are defined and enforced, rather than being indefinite by default.
Check whether classification is applied automatically where it can be, rather than relying on users to label files.
defensive: Define a small number of levels and map each one to concrete technical controls.
Discover where sensitive data actually is, because you cannot protect data you have not found.
Apply classification automatically by pattern or by location, and let users only correct it.
Set retention periods and enforce deletion, because unretained data cannot leak.
Re-classify when data is aggregated, since combining two ordinary records can create a sensitive one.

topics.name: Encryption at Rest, in Transit and in Backup
topics.description: Three places data sits and three separate protections: what full-disk encryption, TLS and encrypted backups each stop, and which access states leave the data readable anyway.

content.overview: Encryption helps in three separate places, and each covers a different failure. Encrypting only in transit leaves the most common leak paths completely unprotected.
how_it_works: In transit protects data while it moves between systems, and this is what HTTPS provides.
At rest protects stored data, so a stolen disk or a compromised storage account does not yield plaintext.
Backups need protection too, because a backup is a full copy of everything you were trying to protect.
Encryption only helps if the key is protected separately from the data, or the two are compromised together.
Full-disk and application-level encryption solve different problems, since one protects a device and the other a specific field.
history: Encryption at rest was expensive and so was applied to databases and backups rather than to laptops.
Storage vendors began offering encryption by default, which removed the cost barrier and the decision.
Cloud platforms added server-side encryption options, often on by default but not always for every service.
Asynchronous replication made it necessary to encrypt backups separately, since a snapshot is a new copy of the data.
real_world: A lost laptop with an unencrypted disk turns into a data breach report, regardless of how good the rest of the system is.
A database with encrypted columns but backups in the clear means the breach simply happens at restore time.
A customer-managed key stored in the same account as the data it protects provides almost no benefit.
what_to_look_for: Check whether encryption is enabled on every store that holds sensitive data, including backups and logs.
Check where the keys live and who can read them.
Check whether backups are encrypted separately from the source system.
Check device-level encryption, since portable devices are the ones that get lost.
defensive: Encrypt everything that holds sensitive data, including backups, replicas and exported extracts.
Keep keys separate from the data, and control key access more tightly than data access.
Enable full-disk encryption on every portable device and require it by policy.
Encrypt data in transit on every connection, including internal ones and backups sent off site.
Verify that a backup is encrypted by restoring from it, rather than by reading the configuration.

topics.name: Malware Families: Viruses, Worms, Trojans, Ransomware
topics.description: Classify malicious code by how it spreads and what it does once it runs — virus, worm, trojan, ransomware — and why modern threats combine several families at once.

content.overview: Malware names describe how something spreads and what it does. Knowing the families is useful mainly because each one implies a different set of controls that would have stopped it.
how_it_works: A virus attaches itself to a file and needs the file to be run, which is why it faded as executable-only systems became rare.
A worm spreads by itself across a network, so containment matters more than detection per machine.
A trojan poses as something legitimate and relies on the user running it, so user-facing controls matter most.
Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment, and its modern form also steals the data first.
Fileless and living-off-the-land techniques run through tools already installed, which is why file-based detection misses them.
history: Early malware relied on floppy disks and shared filesystems, which is why the virus category dominated for decades.
Email and macro-enabled documents created a huge wave of trojans as email replaced physical media.
Polymorphic engines defeated signature detection, and packers were used to hide the real content of a file.
Fileless execution and living-off-the-land techniques shifted the problem toward behavioural detection.
real_world: A worm inside a flat network can reach most systems before anyone notices, which is why segmentation is the main control.
A trojan delivered as an invoice attachment succeeds because the context makes it look expected.
Ransomware that also exfiltrates data gives the attacker leverage even if you restore cleanly.
what_to_look_for: Check that segmentation would actually contain a worm or a ransomware spread.
Check how email attachments and macros are handled, since that is the most common initial delivery.
Check whether behavioural detection is enabled, since file scanning alone misses modern techniques.
Check how quickly you could isolate a machine, because response speed limits most outbreaks.
defensive: Segment the network so a single infected machine cannot reach everything.
Block macros by default and treat attachments from outside the organisation as untrusted.
Use behavioural detection and application control rather than relying on file signatures.
Keep offline or immutable backups, so encryption of the live systems cannot reach the copies.
Practice isolating a machine, because an unproven containment plan does not contain anything.

topics.name: How Malware Gets In: Delivery and Initial Access
topics.description: The two doors every intrusion comes through — a person asked to act, or a flaw left open — and why breaking delivery is the cheapest interruption a defender can buy.

content.overview: Initial access is the step defenders most often miss. If you know how things are getting in, you can remove the route instead of chasing every payload.
how_it_works: Delivery is the mechanism: an attachment, a link, a compromised website, or a malicious update.
The payload then executes with the privileges of whoever opened it, which is usually a person.
Living in memory rather than on disk shortens the window in which a file scan can see anything.
A remote access tool installed afterwards gives persistent hands-on control while looking like a normal tool.
Most intrusions leave a visible trace at delivery, and that trace is the most reliable detection point available.
history: Physical media and unpatched services were the usual routes before widespread internet access.
Email became the dominant delivery channel, and remains so despite years of predictions to the contrary.
Compromised legitimate websites made delivery look like ordinary browsing.
Supply-chain compromise shifted delivery upstream, so the update mechanism itself became the vector.
real_world: A fake invoice with an attachment is still one of the most common first steps in a real intrusion.
An unpatched internet-facing service is often the route, and it is discoverable within hours of appearing.
A third-party update mechanism with broad permissions can distribute malicious code to every customer at once.
what_to_look_for: Check which external services are reachable and what they expose.
Check how email attachments and links are handled, and whether reporting is easy.
Check for software with update rights far beyond what it needs.
Check whether a remote access tool is installed anywhere it should not be.
defensive: Reduce reachable surface first, since an unreachable service cannot be the entry point.
Handle email attachments deliberately: block by default, or require a reason to open.
Give update mechanisms only the permission they need, and monitor what they change.
Alert on remote access software being installed, since that is rarely legitimate.
Make reporting something easy, because speed matters more than perfect filtering.

topics.name: Ransomware: Encryption, Double Extortion and Recovery
topics.description: How ransomware actually denies you your data, why modern operators steal before they encrypt, and which decisions made long before the ransom note decide the outcome.

content.overview: Modern ransomware usually does two things: it encrypts the data and it copies it first. The copy is what creates pressure, because the victim can restore but cannot be sure the data was not taken.
how_it_works: Initial access is followed by a period of quiet activity while the attacker prepares, which is the most useful detection window.
Data is often exfiltrated before encryption, so the theft is complete even if every system is restored.
Encryption then disrupts operations, usually in batches so recovery is deliberately painful.
Backups that share credentials or network access with production are often reached by the same attacker.
Recovery is a business decision under pressure, which is exactly when paying becomes tempting.
