history: Early ransomware encrypted one machine at a time and was largely a nuisance.
Crypto-ransomware made payment meaningful, and criminal groups built around it.
Exfiltration before encryption introduced the double-extortion model and changed the negotiation position.
Ransomware-as-a-service lowered the skill barrier, and affiliate models scaled it.
real_world: An organisation that restores quickly still has to act on the assumption that data was taken.
Backups reachable with the same domain administrator account as production are effectively inside the blast radius.
A network share used for file access can be encrypted far faster than a server, and it is where business data usually lives.
what_to_look_for: Check whether backups are isolated from production in both credentials and network path.
Check whether the backup catalogue itself is protected, since deleting backups defeats everything.
Check how long a full restore would actually take, measured rather than assumed.
Check whether the decision-making path for a ransomware incident is written down and known.
defensive: Keep backups immutable or offline, so encryption cannot reach them.
Use separate credentials for backup administration, so one compromise does not do both.
Test full restores on a schedule and record the real elapsed time.
Segment aggressively, because most ransomware is stopped by containment rather than recovery.
Decide the response criteria in advance, when nobody is panicking, and rehearse it.

topics.name: Backups: The 3-2-1 Rule and Tested Restores
topics.description: Why three copies on two media with one offsite survives ransomware that a synchronised drive does not — and why an untested backup is only a hypothesis about recovery.

content.overview: A backup that has never been restored is a hypothesis, not a control. The rule of three copies is well known; the part everyone gets wrong is the test.
how_it_works: Three copies means the original plus two backups, so one failure is survivable.
Two media means the copies are not all on the same device that can fail together.
One off site means a fire, theft or ransomware at the primary location does not destroy everything.
Incremental and full backups trade speed against restore time, since a restore of many incrementals is slower.
Retention determines what point you can return to, so a ransomware event may exceed the shortest retention.
history: Backups were tape-based, offsite by definition, and slow enough that testing was routine.
Cheap disk arrays made local backups affordable and, with them, the assumption that the copy was safe.
Synchronised storage made replication continuous, which quietly turned a backup into a mirror of the primary.
Ransomware made immutability the main requirement, because anything writable by the attacker is not a backup.
real_world: A synchronised folder is not a backup, since deletion or encryption propagates to the copy immediately.
A restore that has never been timed turns a four-hour outage into a four-day outage.
Backups with a retention shorter than the attacker dwell time can be entirely deleted before anyone notices.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the backup copy is genuinely separate, or synchronised to the primary.
Check whether backups are protected from deletion by the same credentials that run production.
Check the last time a full restore was actually performed and timed.
Check the retention period against the time an attacker could plausibly remain undetected.
defensive: Follow three copies, two media, one off site, and make the off-site copy immutable.
Use separate credentials for backup administration and require multi-factor authentication on it.
Test restores regularly and record the real elapsed time for a full recovery.
Alert on backup deletion, since that is a strong indicator of an ongoing incident.
Include configuration and identity data in backups, since restoring only data often leaves a system unusable.

topics.name: Privacy, Personal Data and Minimisation
topics.description: What counts as personal data, why linkability rather than obvious identifiers decides sensitivity, and why collecting less is the control that removes a whole risk.

content.overview: Data protection law is built on a simple idea: collect and keep only what you actually need. Everything else is liability you chose to take on.
how_it_works: Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable person, which is broader than people assume.
Collecting less reduces the impact of a breach, because there is less to disclose.
Retention limits exposure in time as well as in size, since old data is still a liability.
Sharing with a processor transfers responsibility, which is why contracts and instructions matter.
Individual rights such as access and deletion require the ability to find and remove a person data across systems.
history: Early privacy regulation was sector-specific and focused on records held by organisations.
Broader modern regulation treats data protection as a default across all processing.
Data minimisation moved from a recommendation to an obligation in several jurisdictions.
The practical difficulty of honouring individual rights across many systems is what drives current tooling.
real_world: A marketing database that was never needed becomes the largest disclosure in a breach.
Data retained for a made-up future purpose cannot be justified when a request arrives.
A processor breach becomes your breach from the regulator point of view if you did not control the contract.
what_to_look_for: Check what personal data is actually held, and whether each purpose is still real.
Check the retention schedule and whether anything is kept indefinitely by default.
Check which processors hold data and under what written instructions.
Check whether you could find and delete a specific person data on request.
defensive: Collect only what a stated purpose requires, and write that purpose down.
Set retention periods and automate deletion rather than reviewing manually.
Keep a record of processing so you can answer questions about any dataset.
Use written contracts with processors and verify they are followed.
Build the ability to find and delete a person data across all systems that hold it.

topics.name: Device Security: Locking, Wiping and Mobile/Remote Devices
topics.description: What a lock screen, a locate command and a remote wipe each actually do — how to set them up, how to respond when a device goes missing, and which step cannot be undone.

content.overview: Devices leave the building, and that is the whole problem. Encryption, screen locks and remote wipe only work together, because each addresses a different loss scenario.
how_it_works: Full-disk encryption means a lost device does not leak its contents if it is powered off.
A screen lock and a strong unlock credential are what make that encryption effective in practice.
A PIN or pattern is far weaker than a passphrase, and a short one is brute-forceable quickly.
Remote wipe requires the device to be online and enrolled, so it fails when the device is off or unconnected.
Mobile platforms apply their own protections, but managed-device settings change what an organisation can enforce.
history: Devices were rarely encrypted, and a lost laptop was treated as a lost laptop rather than a data event.
Full-disk encryption became standard on laptops as hardware support matured.
Mobile platforms introduced hardware-backed key storage and strong defaults by default.
Mobile device management added the ability to enforce settings, which only works if the device is enrolled.
real_world: An encrypted laptop with no screen lock is barely better than an unencrypted one, because the key is already in memory.
A four-digit code can be tried quickly enough that a short PIN is effectively no protection.
A device that is out of remote-wipe range cannot be wiped, which is why the recovery plan needs a second step.
what_to_look_for: Check whether full-disk encryption is enabled on every portable device.
Check the screen-lock timeout and whether the unlock credential is a passphrase rather than a short PIN.
Check which devices are enrolled for remote management and which are not.
Check what happens if remote wipe fails, since a second procedure is required.
defensive: Require full-disk encryption and a strong screen lock on every portable device.
Prefer a passphrase over a PIN, and require multi-factor authentication where the platform supports it.
Enrol every device in remote management, and verify the wipe path has been tested.
Keep short automatic lock timeouts, since an unattended device is an unlocked device.
Revoke certificates and sessions on the device when it is lost, so a wipe is not the only defence.

topics.name: Secure Disposal and Sanitisation of Media
topics.description: Why deleting files is not disposal: NIST's clear, purge and destroy categories, how flash media changes the method, and how to verify and record that media is clean.

content.overview: Data that is deleted but still recoverable is not deleted. Disposal has to match the medium and the sensitivity of what was on it.
how_it_works: Deleting a file removes the reference, not the content, and the data usually remains on the medium.
Overwriting can work on a traditional drive but is unreliable on flash and on wear-levelled storage.
Full-disk encryption changes the problem: once the key is destroyed, the data is unrecoverable regardless of the medium.
Physical destruction is the only certain method, and it matters most for small volumes of highly sensitive data.
Retention matters most of all, because a drive that never held the data cannot leak it.
history: Overwriting was the standard method when magnetic drives were the norm and traces were readable.
Flash storage introduced remapping layers that defeat overwriting entirely.
Full-disk encryption shifted the focus to key destruction, which is cheaper and verifiable.
Cloud services made disposal a contractual and logical question rather than a physical one.
real_world: A formatted drive that was encrypted and then had its key destroyed is safe, while a formatted unencrypted drive is not.
Discarded phones and drives are a routine source of data exposure because the wipe was never performed.
A backup provider retaining data past the contract end is a common and easily missed exposure.
what_to_look_for: Check how devices are disposed of, and whether the process is documented and witnessed.
Check whether drives were encrypted, since that changes the correct disposal method.
Check whether backups and cloud copies are included in the disposal process, not just the primary device.
Check for media in recycling and storage that was never processed at all.
defensive: Encrypt every drive that holds sensitive data, so disposal reduces to destroying keys.
Use a documented and witnessed process for any medium that cannot be encrypted.
Cryptographically erase where the platform supports it, and record the certificate that proves it.
Include backups, cloud copies and returned equipment in the disposal process.
Prefer retaining less, because disposal is only necessary for what was kept.

topics.name: How the Web Goes Wrong: The Browser as an Attack Surface
topics.description: Why the browser is the web's largest attack surface: how a response becomes executed code, what the same-origin policy decides, and where the trust boundaries really sit.

content.overview: The browser is where your application meets untrusted input. It also holds the most valuable things a user has: sessions, credentials, and the ability to reach authenticated systems.
how_it_works: The browser renders whatever the server sends, and it has to guess whether that content is data or instructions.
It executes scripts from many origins on the same page, so the origin is the unit of trust.
It stores state in cookies and storage, and that state becomes a target for anyone who can influence the page.
It follows redirects and loads third-party scripts, so a single compromised dependency reaches every user.
The same-origin policy is the main boundary, and most serious web flaws are ways of getting around it.
history: Static pages had no attack surface beyond the server, and the browser was mostly a renderer.
The rise of scripted pages brought cross-site scripting, which remains the most reliable way to act as a logged-in user.
Third-party advertising and analytics scripts became normal, which expanded the trusted computing base of most sites.
Browser sandboxing, site isolation and stronger privacy controls have been added in response to real abuse.
real_world: One compromised third-party script reaches every user of a site, which is a worse distribution channel than any phishing campaign.
A cross-site scripting flaw lets an attacker make authenticated requests as the victim without knowing their password.
A cookie without the right flags is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS flaw becomes full session theft.
what_to_look_for: Check what third-party scripts are loaded, and whether each one is worth the trust it is given.
Check how the response tells the browser to treat the content, rather than relying on the browser to guess.
Check which cookies are readable by scripts and which are sent automatically on every request.
Check whether authentication state is kept somewhere an injected script cannot reach.
defensive: Send explicit headers that restrict what the page may load and do, rather than relying on defaults.
Keep authentication state in cookies that scripts cannot read, with strict scope and lifetime.
Minimise and vet third-party scripts, and prefer ones you can self-host if you genuinely need them.
Use a Content Security Policy in report-only mode first, then enforce it once it is realistic.
Treat any untrusted data reaching a page as a potential XSS payload until output encoding says otherwise.

topics.name: Injection: SQL, Command and Template
topics.description: What injection really is — data reinterpreted as instructions by a SQL, shell or template interpreter — and why parameterised queries remove the confusion instead of filtering around it.

content.overview: Injection is what happens when data is treated as code. It is still one of the most damaging classes of web flaw because it turns data access into code execution, and it is usually a direct consequence of building queries with string concatenation.
how_it_works: A query is code; a value inside it is data. Concatenating a value into the query moves it from data into code.
SQL injection lets an attacker change the meaning of a query, which can mean reading data they should not, changing data they should not, or in some configurations running commands on the server.
Command injection is the same idea against a shell: an argument containing shell metacharacters becomes a command.
Template and expression injection is the same idea again, applied to whatever a templating engine evaluates.
The fix in every case is the same in principle: keep data in a place the interpreter will never treat as instructions.
history: Early web applications built queries by pasting request values into SQL strings, because there was no easier way.
Parameterised queries, called prepared statements, were available early but were not the default in most languages or drivers.
Object-relational mappers made query building convenient and accidentally reintroduced raw-string escaping as a fallback.
Cloud infrastructure as a service removed the easy shell escape, and pushed attackers toward reading data instead.
real_world: A login form built by concatenating the username into a query can be bypassed without knowing any password.
A report feature that shells out to render a file can be turned into arbitrary command execution.
A templating engine evaluating user-supplied expressions turns a template preview into remote code execution.
what_to_look_for: Check whether queries use parameter binding, or whether values are escaped into a string before the query runs.
Check whether a value can influence a table name, column name or sort order, since parameters cannot bind those.
Check for any call that passes user input to a shell, an evaluator or a template engine.
Check whether an ORM raw-query escape hatch is used anywhere near request data.
defensive: Use parameterised queries or prepared statements for every value, and never build SQL by concatenation.
Map any dynamic identifier from a fixed allow-list rather than accepting it from the request.
Avoid invoking a shell; use library calls that take an argument array instead of a command string.
Keep templating engines out of paths where users can supply the template or the expression.
Run the database account with the least privilege it needs, so an injection cannot read or change more than it should.

topics.name: Cross-Site Scripting and Output Encoding
topics.description: Why untrusted data becomes active content in a browser, why encoding belongs at output and to one context at a time, and how sanitisation and safe sinks contain what encoding alone cannot.

content.overview: Cross-site scripting is when attacker-controlled content is treated as script by the browser. It is ranked highly because the script runs with the logged-in user authority, so the attacker never needs a password.
how_it_works: The flaw is a missing decision about what kind of content a value is at the point it is written into the page.
Encoded correctly, a value is text. Encoded wrongly or not at all, the same value can be markup or script.
Reflected scripting delivers the payload in the request, stored scripting saves it on the server, and DOM scripting finds it in client-side code.
Stored scripting is the most damaging because it reaches every visitor and needs no lure.
A cookie scoped to the site is a strong payload: a script that steals it gets the victim authenticated session.
history: Cross-site scripting was one of the earliest named web vulnerabilities and has been a standard top finding ever since.
Modern templating engines introduced auto-escaping, which removed most reflected flaws for teams that used them consistently.
Single-page applications moved rendering into the browser, so flaws moved from the server into client-side code.
Content Security Policy and cookie flags were added as a second layer because encoding alone cannot catch every context.
real_world: A search page that echoes the query without encoding lets an attacker send a link that steals a session when clicked.
A comment stored and later rendered on every page turns one user post into a compromise of every reader.
Client-side code that writes a value into the page with innerHTML reintroduces the flaw despite a safe backend.
what_to_look_for: Check whether output is encoded for the specific context it lands in: HTML body, attribute, URL, JavaScript or CSS are different.
Check client-side code for direct writes of untrusted values into the page.
Check whether the session cookie is readable by scripts, which decides how bad a single flaw becomes.
Check whether a content security policy exists and is actually enforced rather than only reported.
defensive: Encode output for its context, and prefer frameworks that do this by default and only switch off when you must.
Keep session cookies HttpOnly so a script cannot read them even if one gets through.
Deploy a content security policy without unsafe-inline, so injected script is not allowed to run.
Use templating rather than building markup by concatenation, and sanitise where HTML is genuinely required.
Treat content security policy violations as reports to fix, not noise to ignore.

topics.name: Broken Access Control and IDOR
topics.description: Why the identifier in a URL is caller-chosen data, how an insecure direct object reference exposes other people's records, and where the authorisation check has to sit.

content.overview: Broken access control is the top category in the current OWASP list, and the reason is structural: applications grant access in many places, and any one of them being wrong is a breach. Insecure direct object reference is its most common form.
how_it_works: An access decision needs the identity, the action and the specific object, and a check that omits the object is not a check.
A sequential identifier in a URL is an invitation: if /invoice/41 fails, /invoice/42 probably works.
Correct checks are often present on the list page and missing on the detail, edit or delete endpoint.
Client-side hiding of a control is not enforcement, because the request can be sent directly.
Bulk endpoints are especially risky, because one request can act on many objects at once.
history: Early applications assumed a user either saw everything or nothing, so per-object checks were rarely written.
The transition to many customers on one system made per-object checks necessary, and the gap was never fully closed.
The industry survey has ranked broken access control near the top for several editions, and it is first in the 2025 list.
Centralised policy and relationship-based access control are the current direction for avoiding scattered decisions.
real_world: Changing an identifier in a URL returns another customer data, which is one of the most common serious findings in testing.
A delete endpoint with no ownership check lets a user remove records that are not theirs.
An administrative action guarded only by a hidden menu item is reachable by anyone who knows the URL.
what_to_look_for: Check every endpoint that takes an object identifier and ask whether it verifies permission for that object.
Check whether identifiers are guessable, and whether guessing is rate-limited or detected.
Check whether administrative functionality is separated from ordinary functionality, not just styled differently.
Check whether any endpoint accepts an identifier list, since per-object checks are often skipped for bulk actions.
defensive: Default to deny and grant explicitly, so an unimplemented check fails closed rather than open.
Enforce the check on the server for every request, and make it part of the data access layer rather than the route.
Use unguessable identifiers as defence in depth, not as a replacement for a check.
Rate-limit and log authorisation failures, since a burst of them is a clear signal.
Test every endpoint with two accounts of different privilege; this finds these flaws faster than any scanner.

topics.name: Security Misconfiguration and Default Credentials
topics.description: How systems ship convenient rather than safe: default accounts, debug modes, unnecessary services and verbose errors, and how baselines replace configuration-by-habit.

content.overview: Misconfiguration is the second category in the current list, and it is the one most likely to be found by anyone, because it involves no clever technique at all. Default credentials are the extreme case of it.
how_it_works: Every platform ships with defaults, and many defaults are designed to get you running quickly rather than secure.
A service that is only supposed to be reachable internally is often reachable from anywhere because the rule allowing it is too broad.
Verbose errors, directory listings and default paths disclose exactly the information an attacker needs for the next step.
Unnecessary features, sample applications and unused accounts are left in place because removing them was never required.
Configuration drift means the documented secure baseline and the running system quietly stop matching.
history: Manual server configuration meant every machine was slightly different, so nobody could claim to know the state.
Configuration management tools made baselines repeatable and comparison possible.
Cloud platforms moved much configuration to a console, which made it visible but also easy to leave permissive.
Modern platforms increasingly ship secure by default, which raises the value of checking what was changed.
real_world: A database or storage service reachable from the internet with a default account is found within minutes of appearing.
Verbose stack traces disclose framework versions, which narrows the search for applicable weaknesses from years to hours.
A backup or administrative interface left enabled months after a migration is a common finding.
what_to_look_for: Check every service that should not be public, and verify it from outside rather than from inside.
Check for default accounts, sample content and documentation endpoints.
Check error verbosity, since a detailed error is a free reconnaissance tool.
Compare the running configuration against the documented baseline, and fail when they differ.
defensive: Automate a hardened baseline and verify it continuously, because manual checks stop being done.
Remove default accounts, sample applications and unused features as part of installation, not later.
Return generic errors to users and keep the detail in a log the user cannot read.
Restrict administrative and management interfaces to specific addresses and strong authentication.
Fail compliance checks loudly, so drift is caught by the pipeline rather than by an auditor.

topics.name: Vulnerable and Outdated Components: Knowing What You Depend On
topics.description: Why a modern application inherits risk it never wrote: what a CVE describes, and how an SBOM turns dependency risk into a list you can act on.

content.overview: The 2021 list called this vulnerable and outdated components. The 2025 list broadened it into software supply chain failures, because the risk is rarely only in a library you chose yourself.
how_it_works: A dependency you did not write is code you are responsible for, and it is usually a large share of what you ship.
A component advisory matters only in context: if the vulnerable function is never called, the practical risk is different.
Transitive dependencies mean a vulnerability can arrive through something you never named.
A compromised package version is a supply chain attack, and version pinning is what makes it possible.
An unmaintained component will never receive a fix, so exposure grows without anyone choosing it.
history: Component reuse accelerated development and quietly transferred a large amount of security responsibility to third parties.
Software composition analysis tooling made dependency inventories practical and sharply increased the visible number of findings.
Compromised maintainer accounts and malicious package versions turned a maintenance question into a security one.
The 2025 list responded by renaming and widening the category to cover the whole chain rather than the library alone.
real_world: A widely used library maintainer account is taken over, and every application pulling that version is exposed within hours.
An application inherits hundreds of transitive dependencies, and only a generated inventory shows what is actually there.
A component used for a single convenience function can be the largest single risk in the build.
what_to_look_for: Check whether a machine-readable inventory of dependencies exists and includes transitive components.
Check whether advisories are monitored and acted on, and against what prioritisation.
Check build pipelines for unpinned versions and for install scripts that execute third-party code.
Check whether any component is unmaintained, since those will never be fixed.
defensive: Generate a dependency inventory in the build and fail the build on new high-severity findings.
Pin versions and use lock files, so a build is reproducible and cannot silently pull a new version.
Prioritise by reachability: whether the vulnerable code path is actually used in your product.
Remove unused dependencies, since a component nobody uses is risk with no benefit.
Restrict what build steps and install scripts can do, and monitor upstream sources for new advisories.

topics.name: File Uploads, Server-Side Requests and Input Validation
topics.description: Three ways untrusted input reaches further than intended: a uploaded file that becomes something else, a URL the server fetches on a caller's behalf, and validation that checks the wrong property.

content.overview: Input validation, file handling and server-side requests are grouped together because they share one root cause: the application lets untrusted input decide what the server does next.
how_it_works: Validation has to happen on the server, on the parsed value, not only in the browser form.
A file upload is dangerous because the filename, the declared type and the actual content can all differ.
If uploaded files are served from the same origin as the application, a crafted file can run as script against your own users.
Server-side request forgery happens when a URL from a user decides where the server connects, which reaches things the user cannot.
Server-side request forgery is especially useful against cloud metadata services, which return credentials to whoever asks.
history: Client-side validation was long treated as validation, and it protected nothing once the request was sent directly.
Web shells arrived through file uploads, and the fix was separating storage from execution.
Server-side request forgery was named once cloud metadata services made it valuable, and it remains a default-credential route.
Modern frameworks do more validation by default, which helps only where teams use the built-in mechanism.
real_world: An upload directory inside the web root means a crafted HTML or SVG file executes in the site origin.
A preview feature that fetches a user-supplied URL can be aimed at an internal metadata endpoint and return credentials.
A file-type check based on the extension or the client-declared content type is defeated trivially.
what_to_look_for: Check where uploaded files are stored and whether they are served with a content type that cannot execute.
Check whether validation happens server-side, on the value after parsing.
Check every feature that takes a URL and fetches it, and see whether the destination is restricted.
Check whether the fetch follows redirects, since a redirect can bypass an allow-list.
defensive: Store uploads outside the web root, and serve them with a neutral content type and a content disposition of attachment.
Validate on the server against the actual content, not the filename or the declared type.
If the server must render a user file, sanitise it rather than trusting the content.
For server-side requests, allow-list destinations, resolve the address, and re-check after every redirect.
Block access to instance metadata endpoints from application workloads at the network layer.

topics.name: Browser Defences: CSP, HSTS, SameSite and CSRF Tokens
topics.description: What each browser-side control actually stops, why a policy limits damage rather than the bug, and how a CSRF token proves intent rather than guarding a secret.

content.overview: These are the browser-side defences that limit what happens when something else goes wrong. None of them prevents a vulnerability; each of them reduces how much an attacker gets from one.
how_it_works: A content security policy tells the browser which sources of script, style and frames are allowed, so injected script may simply not run.
HTTP strict transport security tells the browser to refuse plaintext, which removes a network-level downgrade.
SameSite on cookies decides whether they are attached to cross-site requests, which is the mechanism behind most cross-site request forgery.
A cross-site request forgery token is a value the attacker cannot read, so a forged request cannot include it.
These controls work together: one blocks the script, one blocks the request, and the other forces the browser to a safe protocol.
history: These headers were added to browsers one at a time, and adoption lagged for years because they broke real applications.
Report-only modes were introduced so sites could measure impact before enforcing, which is the only realistic adoption path.
Modern frameworks enable them by default, which has moved them from an expert concern to a baseline expectation.
Third-party script requirements are the main reason policies stay permissive, which is the same trust problem as before.
real_world: A site with no content security policy turns one stored scripting flaw into a complete account takeover.
A session cookie with no SameSite attribute is sent on cross-site requests, which is exactly what makes forgery work.
HSTS missing from a site allows a network attacker to downgrade the first request, which is often the only one that matters.
what_to_look_for: Check the response headers directly, because configuration that works locally may not reach production.
Check whether the session cookie has Secure, HttpOnly and an appropriate SameSite value.
Check whether a content security policy is enforced or only reported.
Check whether any state-changing action relies solely on a cookie with no token.
defensive: Send a content security policy in report-only mode, fix what it flags, then enforce without unsafe-inline.
Set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on every session cookie, and use the strictest SameSite your flows allow.
Enable HTTP strict transport security, including preloading once you are confident it will not break anything.
Require a token on every state-changing request, and treat the token check as the authorisation check too.
Test with the headers enabled in a real browser, since some failures only appear with a real session.

topics.name: OWASP Top 10:2025 — Reading the List Like a Practitioner
topics.description: What the list groups, what it deliberately leaves out, and how to use it as a shared vocabulary rather than a checklist that ends a review.

content.overview: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document, not a standard. Read it as a map of where real breaches come from, not as a checklist that proves an application is safe.
how_it_works: It is built from data contributed about real applications, so the ranking reflects frequency and impact rather than technical novelty.

The 2025 list is broken access control, security misconfiguration, software supply chain failures, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, authentication failures, software or data integrity failures, security logging and alerting failures, and mishandling of exceptional conditions.
Broken access control is first because it has the widest set of underlying weaknesses, not because it is the most interesting.
Each category points to dozens of specific weaknesses, so the list is an index rather than a description.
A category you are not exposed to is not a category you can ignore entirely, because the same mistake appears under several headings.
history: The first Top 10 was produced from a contributor survey and became the de facto awareness document for web security within a few years.
The 2021 edition reorganised categories and dropped several that were better solved than they once were.
The 2025 edition widened the supply chain category and added a focus on mishandling of exceptional conditions, reflecting observed failure patterns.
It has always been a starting point, and the project says so: the list is awareness, the cheat sheets are practice.
real_world: An organisation that treats a clean Top 10 scan as a security programme has confused a checklist for a process.
The most common findings still cluster in the first two categories, which is why they stay at the top.
The categories cover the web application, so the largest risks in many organisations are entirely outside this list.
what_to_look_for: Use the list to decide what to test and what to build habits around, not to produce a pass or fail result.
For each category, ask whether it applies to what you actually run, and record the reasoning.
Follow the linked cheat sheets, since the list deliberately does not contain the fix.
Treat a finding in a category you were not expecting as a signal that your process has a gap.
defensive: Work the categories in order, because the first two catch more real risk than the rest combined.
Use the cheat sheets and the application security verification standard as your implementation reference.
Add automated checks for the mechanically detectable categories and use manual testing for access control and design.
Feed findings back into code review and pipeline checks so the same category is not rediscovered every quarter.
Keep the list as awareness for a wider audience, and use a more rigorous standard for the work itself.

topics.name: Why People Are Targeted, Not Just Systems
topics.description: Why a person is the cheapest attack surface: what an attacker actually needs from you, the levers they pull, and how the request is designed to bypass every technical control.

content.overview: People are targeted because attacking a person is cheaper than attacking a system, and because a person holds the authority a system will accept. Understanding this is what turns awareness from a lecture into a working instinct.
how_it_works: Social engineering works by creating a situation where the victim applies their own judgement in the attacker favour.
It attacks the decision to trust, not the ability to detect a fake domain or read a header.
Urgency, authority, curiosity and helpfulness are the levers, and each one bypasses a different habit.
A well-researched target is far easier to attack, which is why public information is the preparation stage.
The most effective control is a procedure, because a procedure interrupts the moment of decision in a way awareness alone does not.
history: Early confidence tricks needed only a plausible story, because systems relied almost entirely on physical trust.
The internet removed the need for in-person contact, which made targeting scalable and anonymous.
Social networks turned personal information into a searchable database, which improved targeting quality dramatically.
Organisations moved from awareness campaigns to a behaviour change model, since attendance numbers proved nothing.
real_world: An attacker who knows a target project, manager and holiday dates can build a message that needs no deception at all.
The same request sent to a hundred people in a company usually finds one person with the right combination of access and trust.
Reporting rises immediately after a public incident and then fades, which is exactly when the next wave arrives.
what_to_look_for: Check how decisions are made: if one person judgement is the only control, that person is the target.
Check how much about your organisation is publicly inferable, and whether any of it aids a targeted approach.
Check whether there is a defined process for unusual requests, or whether people improvise.
Check whether people can report something without admitting they were fooled, which determines whether you ever hear about it.
defensive: Put a procedure in front of the decision, so verification happens before action rather than after.
Make out-of-band verification the default for anything touching money, credentials or access.
Reduce the public detail available about who does what, since it is preparation for someone else.
Train on recognition of pressure and urgency rather than on lists of suspicious words.
Make reporting cheap and blameless, because the incidents you never hear about are the ones you cannot measure.

topics.name: Phishing: Anatomy of a Message
topics.description: Read a suspicious message from the outside in — channel, identity, request and context — with the indicators, the layers to check, and the design of a targeted message.

content.overview: A phishing message is a request delivered by a channel you already trust. Learning to read one properly is more useful than learning to spot a bad link, because the link is the part that changes.
how_it_works: The message establishes a plausible context first, so the request feels like a continuation of something already in progress.
A call to action is the point of the message, and everything else exists to make the action seem ordinary.
The sender identity is the easiest thing to fake, and the display name in particular proves nothing.
A link visible text and its real destination are independent, which is why hovering and reading is a real check.
A message that creates urgency or fear reduces the reader willingness to verify, which is the whole objective.
history: Bulk phishing produced a huge volume of obviously bad messages, which trained people to be sceptical at a low threshold.
Spear phishing reduced volume and improved personalisation, which reset that threshold in attackers favour.
Business email compromise refined the approach further by removing any technical trick at all.
Email authentication standards reduced spoofing of the domain, which pushed attackers toward impersonating a real colleague instead.
real_world: A message from a real colleague compromised account is technically perfect, so header and domain checks find nothing.
A password reset prompt that leads to a lookalike domain defeats a user who only checks that the page looks right.
An attachment in a thread the user started, replying to something they actually sent, defeats careful inspection of the thread.
what_to_look_for: Check the actual sender address and reply-to, not the display name.
Check where the link goes before clicking, and prefer navigating to a known address instead.
Check whether the request is urgent, unusual, or bypasses a process you normally follow.
Check whether the message expects you to reveal a credential, a code, or payment details.
defensive: Teach people to hover and read the destination, and to type known addresses rather than follow links.
Require multi-factor authentication so a successful phishing attempt does not mean account access.
Use a separate mailbox for external mail and payment requests, so the ordinary inbox is not the place where trust is tested.
Add a banner marking external or unverified senders, and expect people to read it.
Make reporting a single click, and monitor the report rate as a real security metric.

topics.name: Vishing, Smishing and Quishing
topics.description: Why the channel changed but the attack did not: voice, SMS and QR codes, why caller ID can be spoofed, and the one mobile habit that works everywhere.

content.overview: The same social engineering works over voice, text and QR codes. Each channel has its own weaknesses, and each exploits something different about how people behave in that medium.
how_it_works: Voice works because it creates real time pressure and because the caller can react to what the target says.
A caller who already knows internal terminology, a name or a project detail has credibility immediately.
Text is limited in length, which pushes attackers to use brevity and a single clear instruction.
A QR code moves the target to a physical-looking action, which bypasses the habit of reading a URL before visiting it.
The common thread is a request to change channel, break process, or act before verifying.
history: Cold-calling support desks was an early and effective technique, and largely stopped once verification improved.
Voice phishing returned with the availability of caller identity spoofing and cheap international calling.
Text messaging gained traction once business communication moved to phones.
QR codes created a new delivery channel precisely because scanning does not involve reading an address.
real_world: A caller claiming to be from the service desk, already knowing the employee name, is routinely convincing.
A message about a failed delivery is expected, so a link in it is not surprising.
A code of conduct or parking notice placed in a car park is a genuine lure rather than a mistake.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the caller already knows things they should not, and treat internal knowledge as suspicious rather than reassuring.
Check whether the request moves to another channel, which is the point where the original trust stops applying.
Check whether you are being asked to bypass a process, especially for a supposedly urgent account issue.
Check whether the message arrives on a channel you did not expect to hear from that person on.
defensive: Publish one verified number for the service desk, and instruct staff to call back on it rather than accept an incoming call.
Never ask for a one-time code, password or remote access in response to an unsolicited contact.
Verify payment or credential changes through a channel the requester did not initiate.
Treat an unexpected code of conduct or payment request as a reportable event, not a minor irritation.
Practise the call-back habit explicitly, because it is the control that works across every channel.

topics.name: Pretexting, Baiting and Tailgating
topics.description: The three classic social techniques that need no link and no attachment: the invented scenario, the offered gift and the held door — and the control that answers each.

content.overview: Not every social engineering attack involves a message. Some involve a person walking in, being helpful, or simply following the crowd through a door they should not have opened.
how_it_works: A pretext is a story that explains why the person is asking, and it works when the story fits the situation.
Physical pretexts work in a specific place, so a delivery uniform in a loading bay is more effective than in an ordinary public area.
Baiting leaves something appealing in a place the target will go, turning the target own behaviour into the delivery.
Tailgating needs no deception at all; it relies on someone holding a door and not wanting to make a scene.
All three succeed because the socially correct action and the secure action are different, and the secure one is awkward.
history: Physical access was the original boundary, and it was guarded by a person at a desk.
Access control badges and mantraps replaced the person, which raised the bar for entry.
Organisations moved to self-service and contactless entry, which removed the human checkpoint entirely.
Physical attacks returned as a targeting mechanism once technical entry was hardened, especially against high-value premises.
real_world: An unverified contractor walking through a secure area is a routine and largely unreported event.
A USB drive left in a car park is a low-technology, low-cost and still effective route into an organisation.
Someone carrying an awkward load through a door is accepted without anyone deciding to accept them.
what_to_look_for: Check what your reception process actually does when someone has no appointment, no badge, or no host.
Check whether delivery and contractor entry is separated from general visitor entry.
Check whether anyone challenges an unknown person without needing permission from a manager first.
Check whether there is a defined procedure for a suspicious item found on the premises.
defensive: Make badge-only access the rule, and train staff to challenge rather than to accommodate.
Require escorts for anyone without a business reason to be in the area, including maintenance.
Issue a short, specific procedure for visitors with no appointment, so the decision is not improvised.
Train staff that holding a door is not a security decision they are expected to make alone.
Report anything left or found, since a baited device is only a threat once someone picks it up.

topics.name: Business Email Compromise and Payment Fraud
topics.description: How a hijacked email thread becomes a trusted payment instruction, why the message itself may be technically perfect, and the verification rule that breaks the chain.

content.overview: Business email compromise is the most financially damaging form of social engineering because it involves no malware and no technical flaw. It is a convincing message plus a changed bank detail.
how_it_works: The usual pattern is a thread with a real conversation in it, ending with a request to pay a different account.
The attacker may have read the thread through a compromised mailbox, which is why the context is accurate.
A change of bank details should be the trigger for verification, and the request arrives at exactly the moment that step is easiest to skip.
Payment processes that allow a single person to change details and release payment give the attack somewhere to land.
The loss is often recoverable, but only if it is reported within a short window.
history: Advance fee fraud is the long-running predecessor, and it is still running.
Email account compromise removed the need for any technical skill, since anyone can read a mailbox.
Organisations responded with callback verification procedures, which attackers then learned to work around.
The current model combines mailbox access, a real conversation and a payment process with a single point of control.
real_world: A supplier real mailbox is compromised, and a genuine-looking invoice arrives with new bank details for the first time.
The change is requested during a period of high volume, when verification feels like an obstacle.
An urgent executive request for a confidential purchase bypasses the normal purchase approval route.
what_to_look_for: Check whether any bank detail change is verified by a known phone number rather than by replying to the message.
Check whether payment release and supplier-detail change can be done by the same person.
Check whether executives can request payments that bypass the normal route, and whether anyone verifies them.
Check how quickly a fraudulent payment can be reported and recalled.
defensive: Verify every change of payment details out of band, using a number you already had, not one in the message.
Separate the ability to change supplier details from the ability to release a payment.
Add a defined route for executive payment requests, with a verification step that is always required.
Limit the number of people who can approve payments, and require two for anything unusual.
Rehearse the recall process, because speed is the only thing that recovers the money.

topics.name: Insider Threat: Motive, Opportunity and Detection
topics.description: Insider risk as the authorities actually define it: who counts as an insider, why most insider incidents are not malicious, and how to build controls that detect harm without punishing accidents.

content.overview: The phrase insider threat covers several different situations, and lumping them together leads to bad controls. Malicious insiders and negligent insiders need entirely different responses.
how_it_works: Motive, opportunity and capability are the three factors, and opportunity is the one an organisation controls directly.
Most insider incidents are accidental or negligent rather than malicious, and that changes the whole response.
A departing employee with abrupt behaviour, or one with a grievance, is a recognised risk signal.
Over-broad access makes every mistake and every malicious act far more damaging.
Detection usually comes from a behaviour change relative to a baseline, not from a single action.
history: Early monitoring was limited to what an employee did with a file, which missed data sent to personal accounts.
Data loss prevention tools expanded visibility to email, removable media and cloud uploads.
Analytic platforms made it possible to baseline normal behaviour and alert on deviation.
Legal and privacy constraints in several jurisdictions limit how far behavioural monitoring can go, which is a genuine constraint.
real_world: An employee copying a customer database to a personal drive before resigning is one of the most common insider data events.
A well-meaning administrator bulk-exporting data for a migration creates the same exposure with no intent at all.
A shared account means an insider action cannot be attributed, which blocks the investigation entirely.
what_to_look_for: Check who can reach sensitive data, and whether that matches their current role rather than their history.
Check whether access is removed promptly and automatically when a person changes role or leaves.
Check whether bulk data movement is visible and alerted on.
Check whether actions can be attributed to a person, since shared accounts defeat this.
defensive: Apply least privilege continuously, so no single person can take data they have no business touching.
Remove access automatically on the leaver trigger, and make exceptions visible.
Use unique individual accounts everywhere, including for administrators.
Alert on bulk export and on access to data the person does not normally need.
Handle the negligent case with better tooling and clearer rules, since that is where the majority of incidents are.

topics.name: Building a Reporting Culture and Reporting Channels
topics.description: Why reporting is the highest-value control you have, what makes a channel get used, and how to design one that people trust — including your own, as an individual.

content.overview: You cannot defend against what nobody tells you about. A reporting rate that is implausibly low is a signal about the culture, not about the absence of incidents.
how_it_works: Every report is free information, and every suppressed report is an incident you will learn about later and more expensively.
People hide mistakes when the response to a mistake is worse than the response to an incident.
The reporting channel has to be easier than the alternative of saying nothing.
Reports need to be acted on visibly, or the channel dies.
Time to report is itself a security metric, because it drives how many victims there are.
history: Reporting was rare and often treated as an admission of failure, which suppressed exactly the information defenders needed.
Awareness programmes began to include reporting as an explicit objective rather than a secondary benefit.
Phishing report buttons made reporting a single action, which raised volumes sharply.
Organisations matured to treating reported events as the normal input to detection engineering rather than as a problem.
real_world: A user who clicked a link and did not report it means an entire campaign succeeds because of one non-report.
A team with a low report rate usually has low trust, and often has more incidents than a team with a high one.
A reported suspicious email is often a compromise of somebody else account, so one report protects many people.
what_to_look_for: Check how many people used the reporting channel last month, and whether that number moves at all.
Check what happens to a person after a report, and whether anyone has asked.
Check whether there is a channel that does not require opening a ticket or talking to a manager.
Check whether reports are fed back to the people who made them.
defensive: Make reporting one action, available from email and from the tool bar, with no justification required.
Respond to reports with a visible outcome, even when the outcome is that it was harmless.
Train explicitly that reporting a mistake early is the behaviour being wanted.
Measure report volume, time to report and report quality, and treat a drop as a warning.
Give the security team the authority to act on a report without a management approval step.

topics.name: Security Awareness That Actually Changes Behaviour
topics.description: Why phishing simulations and annual training underperform, what to design instead, and how to measure whether a security programme changed what people actually do.

content.overview: Most awareness programmes measure attendance and satisfaction, neither of which predicts behaviour. The programmes that work change what people do at the moment of decision, and they are usually cheaper than the ones that do not.
how_it_works: Training is most effective immediately before the moment it is needed, and least effective as an annual module.
Feedback that is immediate and personal teaches more than a score, because it connects the action to the outcome.
Simulated exercises work when they are used to measure and improve, and backfire when people are punished for them.
A control that removes the need for a decision beats training for that decision.
Metrics should be behavioural: report rates, verification rates, and how many bad actions were caught by a process rather than by luck.
history: Annual compliance training was the default for years and was widely regarded as ineffective.
Behaviour-based frameworks reframed the objective from remembering rules to performing actions.
Phishing simulations became standard, and were initially used punitively before being corrected.
Current practice pushes the decision upstream: build the process so the error is harder to commit in the first place.
real_world: A team trained annually still falls for the same message, because the training was six months ago.
A callback procedure reduces successful payment fraud more than any awareness course did.
A simulation used to punish people produces under-reporting, which removes the visibility you were trying to create.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the programme measures behaviour or only completion.
Check whether the exercises result in a concrete change, such as a new process or a changed control.
Check whether people are told what to do, not only what not to do.
Check whether the material is specific to the ways your own organisation is actually attacked.
defensive: Prefer a control that removes the decision entirely, and fall back to training only for what remains.
Refresh material on a real incident in your organisation while it is still relevant.
Measure verification and reporting rates, and compare against a baseline rather than against other companies.
Use simulations to improve systems, and never to shame individuals.
Give people a specific script for the two or three situations they are most likely to face.

topics.name: Personal Social Media Footprint and OSINT About You
topics.description: The public information an attacker reads before making contact, how OSINT assembles a targeting picture from open sources, and what you can actually change about your own.

content.overview: Everything an attacker wants to know about you is already public, and the aggregation is worse than any individual post. Reviewing that footprint is the most directly useful thing a person can do for their own security.
how_it_works: Public profiles combine employment, location, relationships and interests into a targeting package.
People search for your data before they contact you, so the search results are part of your security boundary.
A data broker sells the same aggregation to anyone who asks, and organisations often cannot remove it.
Metadata in published photos and documents can disclose location, device and account names.
A strong, reused password tied to an identifiable email address turns a small breach into a targeted one.
history: Personal information was collected mainly by employers, credit agencies and the state.
Social networks made self-disclosure voluntary and constant, and made it searchable.
Data brokers emerged to assemble profiles from those sources, including some that people never knowingly published.
Search engines and people-search services made the assembled profile trivially accessible to anyone.
real_world: A phishing message that references a real conference talk and a real colleague is far more effective than a generic one.
A reused password from a decade-old breach site, applied to an email address with a known employer, is enough for a targeted attack.
Photos of a home office, a badge or a whiteboard disclose more than their owner intended.
what_to_look_for: Search your own name, your email address and your username, and read what is actually indexed.
Check which accounts you have, including ones you stopped using years ago.
Check whether the same password is used anywhere you still care about.
Check what your public posts reveal about location, working hours and relationships.
defensive: Use a different, generated password for every account, with a manager to keep track of them.
Enable multi-factor authentication on the accounts that can reach your email, since email resets everything else.
Review privacy settings on social platforms, and assume anything posted publicly is permanent.
Remove geotags from photographs and check documents for metadata before sharing.
Request removal from data brokers, accepting that coverage is partial and recheck periodically.

topics.name: What Ethical Hacking Is (and the Rules That Govern It)
topics.description: Why ethical hacking is a licence condition rather than a technique set: the same methods, and an authorisation that changes what they mean.

content.overview: Ethical hacking is not a different set of techniques. It is the same knowledge used inside a boundary somebody has explicitly agreed to. The boundary is the entire difference.
how_it_works: The skill set is identical; what changes is whether the owner of the system has consented to the attempt.
Consent is specific: a scope defines which systems, which techniques, and which time window are allowed.
Good intent does not substitute for permission, and an intrusion that helped the owner is still an intrusion without it.
Finding a vulnerability on a system you do not own and reporting it is legitimate only under a defined disclosure route.
Judgement is the part that cannot be taught by tooling, and it is what this whole category is about.
history: The term was popularised as a way to make penetration testing respectable, which it genuinely was.
Structured methodologies emerged so that testing became repeatable and auditable rather than improvised.
Bug bounty programmes turned disclosure into a paid activity, which removed some of the incentive conflict.
Regulators started to expect testing evidence, which moved it from a specialist service to a routine purchase.
real_world: A consultant who finds a serious flaw in a system outside the agreed scope has created a legal problem, not a good story.
A researcher who probes a system hoping to be forgiven is gambling with someone else career.
A test that stops at the first serious finding leaves the owner without a complete picture, which defeats the purpose.
what_to_look_for: Check whether written authorisation names the specific systems, not just the organisation.
Check whether the rules of engagement are documented and understood before any testing begins.
Check whether the person authorising the test actually owns the system, or can authorise the owner to approve.
Check what happens if a test causes an outage, and whether anyone is available to make decisions during it.
defensive: Get authorisation in writing before touching anything, and verify the scope covers each system you intend to test.
Define the rules of engagement up front: methods, time window, contacts, and stop conditions.
Test what you are authorised to test, and report what you find even when it is inconvenient.
Protect any data you encounter, and disclose it through the agreed channel rather than storing or sharing it.
Practise only on systems you own or systems built for the purpose.

topics.name: Authorisation, Scope and the Law
topics.description: The layers a scope document must contain, the parties who must all agree, and why an unwritten permission is not permission at all.

content.overview: Most people who cause real trouble in this field did so by assuming a permission that did not exist. Scope is not paperwork; it is the thing that decides whether your activity is legitimate.
how_it_works: Scope should list every system, by address or domain, and every account you may use.
It should also state what you may not do, because the most damaging actions are the ones nobody wrote down as forbidden.
A time window matters, because testing during production hours has a different risk profile.
Emergency contacts and stop conditions are what turn a mistake into an incident rather than a catastrophe.
Law varies by jurisdiction: an authorisation in one country may not be valid evidence in another.
history: The first computer intrusion laws were written for a few specific cases and did not generalise well.
As testing became commercial, contracts began to carry the authorisation that legislation did not clearly provide.
Computer misuse legislation in several jurisdictions created specific offences for unauthorised access.
Exemptions for good-faith security research were introduced in some places, and they are narrow.
real_world: Testing a third-party hosted service that shares infrastructure with the client can be an offence against someone who never agreed.
Subdomain takeover testing that creates a resource on a shared platform can affect other customers.
Accessing data beyond what was needed to prove a finding can itself be a serious breach, even with authorisation.
what_to_look_for: Check the scope document names targets precisely enough that you cannot be uncertain whether something is in it.
Check whether denial of service, social engineering of staff, and physical testing are explicitly excluded.
Check whether you are permitted to view, download or retain the data you encounter.
Check how disagreements about scope are resolved, and who decides during the test.
defensive: Get a written authorisation that names systems, dates, methods and exclusions.
Confirm in writing that you may not test anything outside the named list, and treat an in-scope doubt as out of scope.
Agree an escalation contact and a stop condition before starting.
Minimise the data you access, and never retain more than the finding requires.
Keep the authorisation with your working notes, because you may need to demonstrate it later.

topics.name: Reconnaissance: Passive and Active
topics.description: Turning a name into a map: what passive research gathers without touching anyone, what active work generates as a side effect, and why the boundary is legal rather than technical.

content.overview: Reconnaissance is how you learn what you are dealing with before touching it. Most of it is legal and unremarkable, and doing it properly removes almost all of the guesswork from later phases.
how_it_works: Passive reconnaissance uses information others have already published: records, certificates, code repositories, job adverts.
Active reconnaissance queries the target directly, which is more informative and is where scope starts to matter.
The goal of the passive phase is a list of assets, technologies, people and attack surface worth confirming.
A job advert, a public code repository or a leaked credential can tell you more than a scan will.
Attackers do exactly this, which is why the same information is your first line of defence.
history: Reconnaissance in the early web era meant reading error pages and directory listings.
Certificate transparency logs made certificate data public, which massively increased passive discovery.
Code repositories and paste sites became a standard place to find credentials by accident.
Search engines indexing of cloud storage misconfiguration turned a single URL into a global exposure.
real_world: An exposed cloud storage bucket is found by a search engine before any scanning is done at all.
A public repository containing a deployment file yields infrastructure names, hostnames and possibly credentials.
A job advert reveals the technology stack, and therefore which defaults to expect.
what_to_look_for: Check what a stranger can learn about your systems without touching any of them.
Check whether certificate, domain and address records expose more infrastructure than intended.
Check whether code repositories, container images and package registries are discoverable.
Check whether current and former staff are findable, and whether that is a problem for you.
defensive: Review what passive reconnaissance reveals about you, and remove what serves an attacker without serving you.
Remove secrets from repositories and rotate anything that was ever committed.
Register only the names you need externally, and manage records deliberately.
Run the same passive collection against yourself, so you know what an attacker sees before one does.
Publish a contact route for researchers, so a finding goes to you rather than to a forum.

topics.name: Vulnerability Assessment vs Penetration Testing
topics.description: The difference between looking for known problems and trying to breach, what each can honestly establish, and why a test is a sample of your process rather than a replacement for it.

content.overview: These are different services with different goals. Confusing them produces either a report full of unexploitable findings, or a test with no coverage record.
how_it_works: A vulnerability assessment is broad and shallow: many checks across many systems, usually automated, producing a prioritised list.
A penetration test is narrow and deep: a small number of systems examined in detail, including logic and chaining, producing evidence of impact.
The assessment tells you what might be wrong. The test tells you what is wrong and what it would cost you.
An assessment answer is roughly how many systems are affected. A test answer is whether the path actually works.
They are complementary, and a common mistake is paying for one and expecting the other.
history: Scanning tools made automated assessment cheap, and the volume of findings became its own problem.
Organisations discovered that a list of thousands of findings was not actionable and started asking for fewer, better ones.
Penetration testing professionalised, with methodologies and reporting standards to match.
Continuous testing emerged to close the gap between a once-a-year assessment and daily change.
real_world: A version disclosed as vulnerable on every host produces a large list and no decision, because none of it is exploitable.
An assessment that never tries chaining misses that a low-severity information leak plus a configuration default equals a full compromise.
A penetration test with no written scope cannot be compared year over year, so the trend is invisible.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the deliverable is a list of findings or a demonstration of impact.
Check how much manual analysis each finding received, and whether the false positives were reduced.
Check whether the scope is written down, since without it you cannot tell what was not tested.
Check whether findings include a realistic attack path rather than isolated issues.
defensive: Run broad assessment frequently and narrow testing periodically, and be honest about which one you are buying.
Require scope and methodology to be documented before work starts.
Ask for findings to be deduplicated and validated, because raw tool output is not an assessment.
Prioritise by exploitability and exposure rather than by scanner severity.
Retest the specific findings you fixed, rather than rerunning everything and re-reading a long report.

topics.name: Scanners, Benchmarks and Interpreting a Report
topics.description: Why automated output is a list of claims rather than a list of findings, how a benchmark differs from a risk, and the four questions that turn an item into work somebody can schedule.

content.overview: A scanner tells you what matches a signature. A benchmark tells you what should be configured. Neither tells you whether your system is actually attackable, and a report of several thousand findings is usually a measurement problem rather than a security one.
how_it_works: Scanners compare configuration and version data against a signature set, so they find what has been written down.
Benchmarks are curated configuration guidance for a platform, usually hardened defaults with justification.
A scan finding is evidence of a possible weakness, not evidence of a vulnerability, until someone confirms it.
The highest-value findings are the small number that combine with something else to create a path.
Coverage matters more than count: a scan of the wrong network tells you nothing about the right one.
history: Network scanners were the original tool, and made regular scanning a routine part of administration.
Web application scanners matured into the dominant source of application findings.
Configuration benchmarks were written to give administrators a defensible target rather than an opinion.
Continuous and agent-based scanning moved the model from scheduled sweeps to live visibility.
real_world: A report of four thousand findings gets triaged to about ten, and the rest is discarded, which is a wasted exercise.
A high-severity finding on a host with no route from the internet is a lower real risk than a medium one on a public host.
A scan that only covers unauthenticated checks misses the misconfigurations that are actually found in the wild.
what_to_look_for: Check whether authenticated scanning was used, since unauthenticated checks see very little.
Check whether the report distinguishes confirmed findings from informational items.
Check whether severity accounts for exposure and not only for the technical severity of the issue.
Check the scan date and whether the estate has changed since.
defensive: Use authenticated scanning, and make the credential a managed one with read-only access where possible.
Tune the signature set to your estate so the report reflects your technology.
Convert a scan into a work queue by grouping findings by control rather than by tool.
Verify high-severity findings by hand before acting, since scanners produce false positives at every severity.
Rescan continuously and alert on the change, rather than reading a monthly report.

topics.name: Exploitation Concepts Without Exploiting Anyone
topics.description: The line between demonstrating a weakness and abusing it: what a proof is allowed to establish, why impact grows one decision at a time, and why the boundary is the actual skill.

content.overview: You can understand exploitation completely without running it against anything you do not own. The concepts transfer; the target does not have to be somebody else system.
how_it_works: Exploitation means turning a weakness into a capability, usually by controlling the instruction pointer or the decision the system makes.
Memory corruption classes differ by what they corrupt: the stack, the heap, or a pointer used as a data value.
Mitigations work by removing the primitives: no-execute pages, canaries, address randomisation and control flow integrity each close a different step.
Logic flaws need none of that machinery, which is why they survive every mitigation.
Post-exploitation is where real damage happens: credential access, discovery, and movement toward what the attacker actually wanted.
history: Stack-based overflows were the dominant exploit class for years, and mitigations were added in response to each wave.
Heap exploitation became necessary as stack protections matured, and it is far harder to reason about.
Modern mitigations shifted towards hardware-enforced control flow, which changed rather than eliminated the problem.
Logic and configuration flaws stayed constant throughout, which is a useful corrective to the focus on memory safety.
real_world: A heap exploitation chain requires several working primitives, so an incomplete mitigation is a real and lasting gap.
Memory-safe languages remove a whole class of bug, but logic flaws in the same code are unaffected.
Most successful intrusions do not need memory corruption at all; they use a default credential or a misconfigured permission.
what_to_look_for: Check whether a memory-safe language is used for the components that handle untrusted input.
Check which exploit mitigations are actually enabled, and on which components.
Check whether the application has logic that assumes input is correct, since that is the class mitigations do not cover.
Check whether any component is a native library without those protections.
defensive: Use memory-safe languages wherever untrusted input is processed, and treat native code as the exception that needs review.
Enable every available mitigation on native components: no-execute, canaries, address randomisation and control flow integrity.
Fuzz the components that parse untrusted input, since memory safety does not cover logic errors.
Review business logic separately, because no mitigation addresses a missing check.
Practise exploitation only in a lab you control, using deliberately vulnerable software built for it.

topics.name: Bug Bounty and Responsible Disclosure
topics.description: How a disclosure programme works: the floor that a policy sets, what a bounty adds, the report format as a two-sided contract, and why the last step is the only one that changes anything public.

content.overview: A bug bounty pays for findings that would otherwise be a gamble. Responsible disclosure is the same activity without the payment. Both are legitimate, and both depend entirely on a defined safe harbour.
how_it_works: A programme states what is in scope, what is out of scope, and what is prohibited, usually including denial of service and social engineering of staff.
Safe harbour is the promise that good-faith research will not be pursued, and without it a researcher is gambling.
Severity is set by the programme, usually based on impact rather than on how clever the technique was.
A report needs reproduction steps, impact, and a suggested remediation, which is what makes it actionable.
Duplicates and out-of-scope submissions are common, so expectations should be set before the work starts.
history: Researchers found vulnerabilities first and had no formal route, so disclosure was public and often disruptive.
Early programmes at large vendors created both a payment model and a written safe harbour.
Platforms aggregated many programmes, which made it possible to hunt across a wide scope as routine work.
Programmes matured to publish response times and scope, which is what makes them usable by outsiders.
real_world: A researcher who tests beyond the stated scope, or causes an outage, can lose the safe harbour protection and face legal action.
A report without demonstrated impact is often triaged low, even when the underlying bug is real.
A programme that never responds teaches researchers to publish instead, which is worse for everyone.
what_to_look_for: Check the scope list before testing anything, and treat anything not named as excluded.
Check the prohibited actions, which usually include denial of service and automated scanning outside a rate limit.
Check whether the programme has an explicit safe harbour and a disclosed response time.
Check how severity is determined, so you know what outcome to aim for.
defensive: Publish a programme or at least a security contact and a safe harbour, even if you do not pay bounties.
State scope and exclusions explicitly, since ambiguity is what causes most disputes.
Commit to a response time, and meet it, because silence is what pushes researchers to publish.
Run a triage process that separates impact from novelty, so researchers optimise for the right thing.
Credit reporters, which is a strong incentive for good behaviour and costs very little.

topics.name: Safe Practice: Lab Environments and Tooling Hygiene
topics.description: Building somewhere it is safe to be wrong: isolation, identity, data and network boundaries, and the habits that keep a practice machine from becoming anyone's problem.

content.overview: Everything you want to practise on exists as a deliberately vulnerable system you can run yourself. Practising on anything else is both unsafe and, for the skill, less useful.
how_it_works: Deliberately vulnerable systems exist to be broken, and they are built so that breaking them is safe and repeatable.
Isolating the lab on a host-only or internal network means a mistake cannot reach anything real.
Snapshots let you reset in seconds, which removes the reason people keep practising on live systems.
