The tools you install for testing are themselves an attack surface, so they are worth handling carefully.
Anything you capture in a lab is still real evidence, so treat lab data as if it were sensitive.
history: Training environments were once assembled by hand from deliberately old software, which worked and was painful.
Prebuilt vulnerable systems made it possible to start in minutes rather than days.
Virtualisation and container platforms made resetting an environment nearly free.
Current practice increasingly uses infrastructure-as-code so a lab is described rather than assembled.
real_world: A test tool installed with default credentials is itself a route into the machine it runs on.
A lab with default network bridging can reach the real network the moment a mistake is made.
Captured credentials and tokens from a lab get reused, because they look like ordinary credentials.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the lab is isolated from any network you care about, and verify rather than assume.
Check whether the test tooling is from a trusted source and is kept current.
Check whether you have a way to reset quickly, because time pressure causes mistakes.
Check that you know which of your own accounts and credentials you are using in the lab.
defensive: Run labs on a host-only or dedicated internal network, with no route to production.
Snapshot before each session so you can reset instead of trying to undo damage.
Download tooling only from the official source, verify what you run, and keep it updated.
Use separate, throwaway credentials inside the lab, and never reuse a real one.
Document the lab setup so you can rebuild it, and so the next person does not rebuild it badly.

topics.name: From Finding to Fixing: Writing a Usable Report
topics.description: Why a report is a work order rather than a trophy: the five layers a finding needs, the decisions that stay with the organisation, and the question that makes the next one cheaper.

content.overview: A finding nobody can act on is a finding that will not be fixed. The report is the deliverable, and its quality matters more than the sophistication of how the issue was found.
how_it_works: A usable finding states the impact in the owner terms, not in the researcher technique.
Reproduction has to be reliable and quick, because the first person to verify it decides whether it gets fixed.
Evidence should show the problem occurred, not merely that a scanner thought it might.
A specific remediation is worth more than a general principle, because the owner has to decide what to change.
Severity should be argued from impact and exposure, and the argument should be visible in the report.
history: Early penetration test reports were long narratives, which read well and changed very little.
Standardised report formats emerged so that findings could be tracked to closure across teams.
The industry moved toward a common weakness classification, which made severity comparable between tools and reports.
Bug bounty platforms imposed short structured templates, which is why most modern reports are structured.
real_world: A report with twenty pages of narrative and no reproduction steps gets closed as unverifiable.
A one-page report with a clear impact statement and a specific fix gets fixed.
A severity argument based on scanner rating alone is easily overruled by a team that knows their own exposure.
what_to_look_for: Check whether every finding has reproducible steps that a sceptical person can follow.
Check whether impact is stated in business terms rather than only in technical ones.
Check whether the recommendation is specific enough to be turned into a change.
Check whether the severity reflects this environment exposure, not just the issue in the abstract.
defensive: Track findings in one place with an owner and a due date, and review open ones regularly.
Retest what you fixed and close on evidence rather than on the developer word.
Write the report so a busy person can act in five minutes: summary, impact, reproduction, fix.
Feed recurring findings back into code review and pipeline checks so the category does not return.
Accept that not everything gets fixed, and record the accepted risk explicitly rather than silently.

topics.name: The Defender's Loop: Prepare, Detect, Contain, Eradicate, Recover
topics.description: The shape of defensive work: what each stage of the incident loop actually involves, and why the order is a set of judgement calls rather than a checklist.

content.overview: Incident response is a loop, not a line. The value is in coming back around with the thing you learned and making the next pass cheaper.
how_it_works: Preparation is everything done before an incident: the playbooks, the access, the logging and the contacts.
Detection is the moment you become aware, and the gap between compromise and awareness is the number that matters.
Containment stops it spreading without destroying evidence, which is a genuine tension rather than a contradiction.
Eradication removes the cause, which is not the same as cleaning up the symptoms you found.
Recovery restores service, and lessons learned only count if they change something concrete afterwards.
history: Response was initially improvised by whoever discovered the problem, which rarely went well.
Formal playbooks arrived so that roles and steps were defined before the pressure was on.
The realisation that most incidents repeat turned post-incident work from optional into the main driver of improvement.
Current practice treats the loop as continuous, with detection engineering feeding directly into the playbooks.
real_world: Most organisations can contain quickly and recover slowly, and the recovery step is where the outage actually happens.
An incident closed without a documented cause leads to the same incident again within a year.
A playbook nobody has rehearsed is a document, not a capability.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the plan is written down and whether the named people still work there.
Check how long it takes to detect, to contain and to recover, and whether those numbers are measured or assumed.
Check whether anyone has authority to make decisions during an incident without waiting for a meeting.
Check what happens to the evidence, because that decision is often made by accident.
defensive: Write the playbook before you need it, and rehearse it with the people who will actually run it.
Measure detection and containment times, since they are the numbers that improve when you practise.
Name a decision-maker for out-of-hours incidents and define what they can authorise.
Record the root cause, and require an owner and a date for every corrective action.
Feed the lessons back into the playbook rather than into a report nobody opens.

topics.name: Logs and Telemetry: What to Collect and Why
topics.description: Turning a question into a log source: what a defender needs to see, which log establishes what, and the collection mistakes that make good telemetry useless.

content.overview: Logs are the raw material of every investigation. The design question is not what you can log, but what you will need in six months when you do not yet know what you are looking for.
how_it_works: Collection is only useful if it survives the attack, so logs need to live somewhere the compromised host cannot reach.
Log integrity matters: an attacker who can edit a log can mislead the investigation.
Retention is a real trade-off between disk cost and the window in which you might need the data.
Time synchronisation decides whether records from different systems can be correlated at all.
Context matters as much as events: an event without the user, source and outcome is hard to act on.
history: Local logging was controlled by whoever owned the machine, which meant an administrator could erase their tracks.
Central collection solved that and created a new problem: far more data than anyone reads.
Structured logging formats made cross-source correlation practical for the first time.
Current practice treats log data as a security asset with its own access controls and lifecycle.
real_world: An investigation stalls because authentication records for the relevant week were never collected.
A system whose clock drifted produces a timeline that looks plausible and is wrong.
Logs stored on the same host as the compromised application are gone by the time anyone looks.
what_to_look_for: Check which events are actually collected, and whether successful logins are included as well as failures.
Check whether a local administrator can delete or alter the logs you rely on.
Check the retention period against the longest window an investigation might realistically need.
Check clock synchronisation across every system whose records you intend to correlate.
defensive: Centralise collection so host compromise cannot erase the record.
Log authentication, privilege changes, administrative actions and outbound connections, not just errors.
Synchronise time across systems, and treat drift as a monitoring alert.
Protect log storage with its own access controls and integrity checking.
Set retention deliberately and make it visible what is kept and for how long.

topics.name: SIEM, Alerts and Tuning Out Noise
topics.description: How a detection becomes a decision: what alerting is for, why an untrusted alert is worse than none, and how tuning turns a rule from a hypothesis into a piece of evidence.

content.overview: A SIEM collects everything and therefore alerts on whatever someone configured. The work is deciding what deserves a human, and the honest answer is usually a small fraction of what fires.
how_it_works: A detection rule encodes a hypothesis about attacker behaviour, and its quality is the quality of that hypothesis.
A rule that fires on common activity produces alert fatigue, and alert fatigue is functionally the same as no detection.
Coverage should be measured against known techniques rather than against the number of rules deployed.
Tuning is continuous: an environment baseline changes, so a rule that was rare becomes common.
The measure that matters is how long a true positive takes to reach a person who can act.
history: Early correlation engines were log-file filters that produced little more than grep with a schedule.
Rules migrated into platforms as regular expressions, which made detection easy to write and hard to maintain.
The volume of alerts became the dominant problem, and organisations started measuring false positive rates deliberately.
Detection engineering and behaviour analytics moved the goal from more rules to more coverage.
real_world: A queue with thousands of open alerts is read by nobody, and the rule is present on a compliance slide.
A rule written for a specific incident and never generalised catches that incident once.
An alert with no documented response is a notification, and notifications do not reduce risk.
what_to_look_for: Check how many alerts are open, how old they are, and how many were true positives.
Check whether each alert has a documented first action, and who performs it.
Check which attacker techniques you have any coverage for at all.
Check how long a real alert took to reach a responder, measured rather than estimated.
defensive: Measure coverage against a behaviour framework, so gaps are visible rather than assumed absent.
Give every alert a documented first action, and delete the ones that have none.
Tune continuously using the false positive data you already generate, rather than in a one-off project.
Prioritise alerts by the technique they indicate, so triage starts from impact.
Track time to detect and time to respond as the primary metrics, since they predict outcome better than rule count.

topics.name: The MITRE ATT&CK Framework for Defenders
topics.description: ATT&CK as shared vocabulary: tactics, techniques, data sources and detections, and the honest limits of a knowledge base that describes what attackers do.

content.overview: ATT&CK is a shared vocabulary for what attackers actually do. For defenders its main value is coverage: it turns the vague goal of being secure into a checklist you can measure yourself against.
how_it_works: A technique describes behaviour an adversary uses to reach an objective, and each has sub-techniques describing specific implementations.
Tactics are the reason for the technique, so the same technique may appear in different phases for different goals.
Software, industry and the adversary groups are published as separate matrices, which lets you compare your own relevance.
Mapping your detections to techniques makes coverage explicit and gaps arguable rather than invisible.
The framework is descriptive, not prescriptive: it tells you what is possible, not what is likely against you.
history: It began as a way to document adversary behaviour from incident reports, because the knowledge existed only in people heads.
Organisations adopted it as a detection reference, and the detection and platform matrices followed.
Public incident reporting across sectors made the data set large enough to be genuinely representative.
It is now used for threat modelling and for procurement, as well as for detection coverage.
real_world: A team with five hundred detection rules can still have no coverage of the techniques actually used against their sector.
Coverage measured by rule count is meaningless; coverage measured by technique is at least arguable.
Adversaries choose the technique that works against the defences in front of them, so they route around gaps.
what_to_look_for: Check which techniques relevant to your sector you have visibility into, and start with the ones you lack entirely.
Check whether your detections produce usable context, since a technique alert with no detail is not actionable.
Check which sub-techniques you cover, because the specific implementation varies by group.
Check when your coverage was last reviewed, since it decays as systems change.
defensive: Map your logging and detections to techniques, and treat unmapped techniques as the work list.
Start with the techniques most common against your sector rather than the most famous ones.
Use the framework to explain gaps to non-specialists, since the vocabulary is widely understood now.
Review coverage on a schedule, because a change in estate silently reduces it.
Use it for detection engineering and threat modelling, and ignore the parts you have no use for.

topics.name: Incident Response: Roles, Severity and Communication
topics.description: Who decides, who says what and to whom: the roles an incident needs, why severity is a business judgement, and how communication is a control rather than a courtesy.

content.overview: Most incident response failures are coordination failures rather than technical ones. Knowing who decides, who talks and who is told is worth more than knowing any particular tool.
how_it_works: Roles are usually incident commander, technical lead, communications and scribe, and the separation matters more than the titles.
The incident commander makes decisions and does not investigate, because doing both reliably is not possible under pressure.
One person communicates outward, so the internal team is not answering questions while working.
Severity has to be defined in advance, because deciding during the incident biases towards under-calling it.
Legal, privacy and regulatory notification obligations usually run on their own clocks, independent of the technical work.
history: Response was once a small group of people who all knew the systems and each other.
Organisations grew and the ad hoc approach stopped scaling, so formal roles were introduced.
Distributed work made written communication necessary, since the conversation could no longer happen in one room.
Current practice treats communication as a deliverable with its own owner, not as something that happens by accident.
real_world: The technical lead starts fixing things and stops directing, and the incident loses its coordination.
A statement goes out describing an incident that later turns out to be different, which is hard to walk back.
A regulatory deadline passes because nobody owned the notification decision.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the plan names a commander, a technical lead and a communications owner.
Check whether severity levels have defined criteria and who is allowed to declare them.
Check whether the out-of-hours contact list is current and has been tested.
Check whether the notification decision path is documented, including who can start the clock.
defensive: Define roles and name the people who fill them, with a named deputy for each.
Write severity criteria in advance and require the higher severity when uncertain.
Give the incident commander the authority to make decisions without convening anyone.
Keep a written timeline during the incident, because reconstructing it afterwards is much harder.
Practise the communication path at least once, including the awkward conversations with legal and customers.

topics.name: Forensics Basics and Evidence Handling
topics.description: Acquiring, preserving and working with evidence: why a verifiable copy matters, what order of volatility is for, and how a defensible record is built from the moment you touch a system.

content.overview: Forensics is what you do with the data you preserved. The order of operations matters enormously, because the first action taken often destroys the evidence you would have needed.
how_it_works: Live memory holds evidence that is gone the moment the machine powers off, so that decision comes first and is irreversible.
Imaging a running system is not perfect, which is why containment decisions have to be made consciously.
A write-blocked copy preserves the original; analysing the original directly is how evidence gets contaminated.
Hashing and timestamping establish an integrity record that survives a challenge later.
Chain of custody exists so the evidence is admissible, which is a legal requirement rather than a technical one.
history: Early forensics was disk-level and destructive, which meant investigating meant destroying the evidence.
Write blockers and disk imaging made non-destructive analysis possible.
Memory forensics became practical and changed what could be recovered after a compromise.
Cloud and containerised systems changed the model again, because there is often no disk to image.
real_world: Rebuilding a machine before imaging it destroys the memory and the temporary files that explained the intrusion.
Running antivirus on an infected host before imaging changes the very files being investigated.
Evidence held without a custody record can be excluded, however conclusive it was.
what_to_look_for: Check whether your response plan starts with preservation, or with containment that destroys evidence.
Check whether you can acquire a full memory capture on the platforms you run.
Check whether the imaging and custody process is documented and repeatable.
Check whether you have somewhere to store evidence securely for as long as it may be needed.
defensive: Decide the preservation order in advance and write it into the playbook.
Capture memory before power-off on systems where that evidence matters, and accept the trade-off consciously.
Image with a tool that hashes as it writes, and keep the original read-only.
Record every transfer of evidence, with who handled it and when.
Practise acquisition on a lab machine, since the first real attempt should not be the first attempt.

topics.name: Containment, Eradication and Lessons Learned
topics.description: The judgement calls that decide an incident's outcome: how to contain without destroying evidence, how to know an intruder is actually gone, and how to turn the review into a change.

content.overview: Containment is a decision under pressure with real trade-offs, and getting it wrong is more expensive than getting it slow. Eradication is where most teams stop too early.
how_it_works: Short-term containment is fast and reversible, such as isolating a host or disabling an account.
Long-term containment is slower and more durable, such as rebuilding rather than cleaning.
Cleaning a compromised system is unreliable because you cannot prove you removed everything, which is why rebuilding is preferred.
Eradication includes closing the entry point, not only removing what is already there.
Recovery is validated, not assumed: service restored is not the same as service trustworthy.
history: Early response guidance leaned towards cleaning, on the reasonable assumption that attacks were visible.
Persistence mechanisms that are easy to miss made cleaning unreliable, and the guidance moved to rebuild.
Ransomware made the point concrete, because recovery time matters more than elegance when business is down.
Current practice treats recovery verification as a distinct step rather than part of restoring service.
real_world: A host returned to the network with the original persistence still present, and the same intrusion continued.
Rebuilding from an image that already contained the compromise repeats the problem exactly.
Service restored quickly and a second incident follows within a day.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the plan prefers rebuild over clean, and whether the option to rebuild actually exists at speed.
Check how you confirm eradication, rather than assuming the absence of symptoms means it is gone.
Check whether rebuilds come from a source you trust, since a compromised image reproduces the compromise.
Check how recovery is validated before a system is trusted again.
defensive: Rebuild from a known-good image rather than cleaning, and keep rebuild time measured.
Close the entry point as part of eradication, not as a separate task someone forgets.
Monitor rebuilt systems for the same indicators before declaring them clean.
Validate recovery with a defined check before returning the system to service.
Hold a blameless review with a named owner and a date for every corrective action.

topics.name: Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery and Resilience
topics.description: The plans that exist for the day the systems do not: what continuity and recovery each promise, how the objectives are set, and why an untested plan is not a plan.

content.overview: Security and availability are usually in tension, and resilience is the discipline that resolves it. The question is not whether you can prevent everything, but whether you can keep operating while you deal with what you cannot prevent.
how_it_works: Business impact analysis establishes which services matter most and what their tolerable downtime is.
Recovery time and recovery point are different questions, and a plan has to answer both for each service.
Resilience means surviving degradation, not only avoiding failure, so a reduced mode of operation should exist.
Plans fail because of assumptions about systems and people that are no longer true.
Exercises test the plan, and an untested plan is a document with good intentions.
history: Continuity planning started as disaster recovery for datacentres, focused on restoring hardware.
It broadened to include processes and people, which is where most real disruption actually lands.
Cloud services changed the recovery options without changing the underlying questions.
Resilience became a board-level concern as dependence on digital services increased.
real_world: A business that can operate manually for two days has far more options than one that cannot.
A ransomware event where staff cannot be paid or customers cannot be reached becomes a business problem, not a technical one.
A plan that lists a recovery time no supplier has ever committed to is fiction.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the plan names recovery times per service and whether they were agreed with the business, not only with IT.
Check whether a reduced manual mode is defined and has been practised.
Check what the plan assumes about staff availability, since that assumption breaks during an incident.
Check when the plan was last exercised and what the exercise found.
defensive: Agree tolerable downtime per service with the business owner, in writing.
Define and rehearse a manual mode for the services where downtime is most damaging.
Exercise the plan with the people who would run it, including outside working hours.
Reconcile the plan against actual supplier commitments at least annually.
Treat availability decisions as security decisions, since they are usually the same decision.

topics.name: Threat Intelligence: IOCs, TTPs and KEV
topics.description: What a piece of threat intelligence can and cannot tell you, why indicators expire and techniques do not, and how a known exploited vulnerability changes what you do on Monday morning.

content.overview: Threat intelligence is only useful when it changes a decision. Indicators tell you what to look for now; techniques tell you what to build; the exploited catalogue tells you what to patch first.
how_it_works: An indicator is a specific artefact: an address, a domain, a file hash. It is precise and expires quickly.
A technique is behaviour: how the adversary achieves something. It is durable and useful for design.
The known exploited vulnerabilities catalogue is a small, high-confidence list of weaknesses being used in the wild.
Intelligence has to be mapped to your estate, or it is just someone else incident report.
A feed you do not act on adds cost and false confidence, which is worse than having no feed.
history: Intelligence started as a commercial feed industry selling indicator lists that were frequently stale.
Realised value came from understanding the adversary behind the indicators, not the indicators themselves.
Frameworks such as ATT&CK gave the durable layer that survives the indicator churn.
Government catalogues of actively exploited vulnerabilities have made prioritisation concrete for everyone.
real_world: A blocklist updated weekly stops campaigns that started years ago and does nothing about current ones.
An exploited catalogue entry for a library buried in a build turns a general patch problem into a specific task.
Intelligence shared in a machine-readable format is usable; intelligence in a PDF is an article.
what_to_look_for: Check whether consumed intelligence has led to a specific change, and find the last one.
Check whether your exploited-catalogue monitoring covers the products you actually run, including libraries.
Check whether your estate data is current enough to make an indicator useful at all.
Check how you evaluate a source, since an unrated feed is an unverified claim.
defensive: Prioritise the actively exploited catalogue above severity scores, since it reflects real attacker behaviour.
Consume intelligence in a machine-readable format and feed it into detection and blocking automatically.
Map adversary techniques to your detections, which is the part of intelligence that keeps its value.
Score sources and drop the ones that never produce a useful indicator.
Review what changed because of intelligence each quarter, and stop consuming anything that changes nothing.

topics.name: The Threat Landscape Today: Ransomware, C2, Supply Chain
topics.description: Ransomware, command and control, and the software supply chain read as three mechanisms rather than three headlines, with the sources that track them and the controls that answer each.

content.overview: The threat landscape is not one thing. What matters for you depends on your sector, your size and what you are worth, and the most useful question is which of the common patterns is actually aimed at organisations like yours.
how_it_works: Ransomware remains the most visible cause of disruption, and the exfiltration-first model is now the norm.
Initial access is usually a person, a default credential or an unpatched internet-facing service, not a novel technique.
Command and control increasingly blends into normal traffic, which makes network blocking alone insufficient.
Supply chain compromise is lower frequency but very high impact, because trust is extended to whoever you depend on.
Most organisations are not targeted by name; they are reached because they are exposed, which means exposure is the thing to fix.
history: Mass indiscriminate malware made volume the main problem, and it largely peaked.
Organised criminal groups emerged, running ransomware and initial access as a service business.
Extortion shifted to include the data itself, which changed the leverage entirely.
Current activity combines all of the above, and the defensive implication is that containment and recovery matter as much as prevention.
real_world: An unpatched internet-facing appliance is compromised within days of appearing, routinely and without targeting.
A criminal affiliate buys access to one organisation and reuses it across many others in the same sector.
An organisation that can rebuild quickly from clean backups negotiates from a position that most never reach.
what_to_look_for: Check which of the common intrusion paths are open for you: exposed services, default credentials, unmanaged devices, email.
Check whether your backups are reachable with the credentials production uses.
Check how long it would take to rebuild a core system, since that number decides the outcome more than prevention does.
Check what your sector is specifically targeted for, since it changes the priority order.
defensive: Remove internet exposure that serves no purpose, which removes the most common entry point at zero cost.
Monitor the actively exploited catalogue against your actual estate, including what is buried in dependencies.
Assume exfiltration happened, and design backups on the assumption the attacker will reach them too.
Segment so a single compromised account does not reach everything.
Rehearse recovery, because response time is the variable you still control when everything else has failed.

topics.name: Standards and Frameworks: NIST CSF, CIS, ISO, SOC 2
topics.description: A law, an attestation, a framework, a benchmark and a standard are different kinds of document answering different questions, and reading one as another is the most common framework mistake there is.

content.overview: Frameworks exist to stop you inventing your own vocabulary. The honest position is that none of them is the answer, and that using one properly beats knowing several superficially.
how_it_works: The cybersecurity framework is organised as govern, identify, protect, detect, respond and recover, and it is deliberately outcome-based rather than control-based.
The centre for Informed Security controls give a prioritised, tiered set of concrete safeguards with implementation detail.
The international standard is certifiable and is what most regulated and supplier-assessed organisations are held to.
A service organisation control report is an attestation against trust services criteria, not a certification of security.
Frameworks overlap heavily; the useful move is to choose one as the primary structure and map the others into it.
history: The cybersecurity framework began as a response to the fragmentation of American critical infrastructure regulation.
Its second version added governance explicitly, acknowledging that most risk is not technical.
The centre for informed security controls moved to tiered safeguards, which made prioritisation explicit.
Certification pressure drove adoption more than practical utility did, which is a fair criticism of several of them.
real_world: A supplier questionnaire asks for one framework, and answering it in the wrong vocabulary costs a week each time.
An audit against a tiered control set produces a short, prioritised list, which is far more actionable than a generic assessment.
Adopting three frameworks fully is not possible; adopting one and mapping the others is.
what_to_look_for: Check whether one framework is the primary language your reporting and audits already use.
Check whether the framework version is current, since the frameworks themselves have changed materially.
Check whether the controls you selected are actually implemented and verified, rather than documented.
Check how you will evidence the controls, since unevidenced controls do not survive an assessment.
defensive: Pick one framework as the spine of your programme and map everything else into it.
Use the tiered approach where it exists, so effort goes to the controls that reduce the most risk first.
Implement a control fully rather than documenting many partially.
Verify controls continuously rather than at audit time, since unverified controls are assumptions.
Keep evidence as a by-product of the work rather than as a separate documentation exercise.

topics.name: Compliance and Privacy Law at a Practical Level
topics.description: What a legal duty actually does to an engineering team: what has to be designed in, what has to be recorded, and where a technical person's competence ends. Practical, not legal advice.

content.overview: Compliance is a floor, not a ceiling. It tells you what you must do and by when, which is genuinely useful, and it tells you nothing about whether you are actually secure.
how_it_works: Obligations come from law, from contracts, and from sector regulators, and they overlap without agreeing.
Privacy law is built around a lawful basis for processing, a notice obligation and individual rights, rather than around security controls.
Security obligations are usually about process: what you must be able to show, and how quickly you must respond.
Cross-border transfers have their own rules in several jurisdictions, which affects any global service.
Contractual requirements from customers are frequently stricter than any legal obligation, and are the ones you will actually be held to.
history: Early regulation was sector-specific and focused on record keeping rather than on technology.
Broader privacy regulation introduced the concept of a lawful basis and made minimisation an obligation.
Breach notification rules put a clock on the response process, which changed how incident response is written.
Current enforcement is increasingly about what you did versus what you documented, which makes the documentation the evidence.
real_world: An organisation is fully compliant with every control and still suffers a breach, because compliance never claimed otherwise.
A contractual security questionnaire from a large customer imposes requirements the law does not.
A breach notification deadline passes because the decision to notify was never assigned to a person.
what_to_look_for: Check which regulations actually apply to you by size, sector and location, rather than assuming.
Check your notification obligations and their clocks, and who owns the decision.
Check what your customer contracts require, since they are usually the strictest thing you are held to.
Check whether you can evidence your controls to a standard an auditor would accept.
defensive: Maintain a short, accurate record of which obligations apply and why, reviewed when you change jurisdiction or sector.
Build the notification decision path into the incident playbook with a named owner.
Treat contractual security requirements as the baseline to design against, since they are the strictest and most enforced.
Keep evidence generation as part of the normal control operation.
Use compliance to structure the work honestly, and be explicit with leadership about what it does not cover.

topics.name: Risk: Likelihood, Impact and Talking to Management
topics.description: Turning a technical finding into a decision: risk statements, the two multipliers, and the three sentences that get a resource decision made in the room.

content.overview: Risk is the only currency in which a security decision gets made. The point of the exercise is not to compute a number; it is to make the comparison between risks explicit enough to argue about.
how_it_works: Risk is likelihood multiplied by impact, and both terms are estimates that reflect your own organisation, not an abstract score.
Impact has several dimensions: money, customers, regulatory, and personal, and they rarely rank the same way.
A risk register is only useful if it drives a decision, and most do not because nothing is ever retired from them.
Inherent risk is what exists before controls; residual risk is what remains after them, and only residual matters for the decision.
Risk acceptance is a legitimate outcome and should be recorded by a named person, not left implicit.
history: Risk registers arrived as compliance artefacts in regulated industries.
Quantitative approaches promised precise numbers and mostly produced false precision, and largely lost favour.
Current practice leans towards qualitative, comparative scales used consistently rather than numerical ones.
Risk appetite, agreed at board level, is what makes the individual decisions easier.
real_world: A register with two thousand entries and no prioritisation is a document, not a management tool.
A control chosen because it was cheap rather than because it reduced risk fills the register without reducing anything.
A risk accepted silently by one person is invisible to everyone who later needs to know.
what_to_look_for: Check whether risk is expressed in your own environment rather than generic scores.
Check whether anything on the register has been removed, which tells you whether it is a live document.
Check whether risk owners are named individuals rather than departments.
Check whether the top risks are reflected in current investment decisions.
defensive: Keep the register short enough that it can be read, and rank it explicitly.
Use one consistent scale and apply it the same way every time, since comparability matters more than precision.
Name an owner for each risk and record who accepted it and when.
Review the register on a schedule and remove anything that is no longer a risk.
Report the top few risks and the decisions taken on them, rather than the whole document.

topics.name: Building a Home and Small-Business Security Program
topics.description: A security programme a two-person organisation can actually run: what to do in the right order, which habits do the most work, and what not to buy first.

content.overview: Most of the serious attacks on small organisations and home setups are opportunistic rather than targeted. A small number of habits removes most of that exposure, and the habits are not expensive.
how_it_works: Small environments have the same weaknesses as large ones and none of the defences, so defaults are the real risk.
Automatic updates on everything reachable from the internet is the single highest-value action.
Administrative separation matters even at home, because it stops a compromised everyday account reaching everything.
Backups on a separate medium, tested occasionally, are what distinguish a bad day from a bad month.
The people who run small environments are also the people who must respond to an incident, which is a capacity problem.
history: Home and small business computing was consumer-grade and assumed the router was the boundary.
Cloud services moved most of the estate off-premises, which removed the boundary but added account risk.
Ransomware shifted from targeting organisations to targeting whoever is reachable, including home machines.
Remote work made home networks business networks, which removed the distinction entirely.
real_world: An unpatched router or camera is compromised and used to reach devices inside, which is routine and automated.
A reused password on a service that holds your email is the most valuable credential you own.
A backup on the same device as the original protects against nothing except accidental deletion.
what_to_look_for: Check what is reachable from the internet, including remote access tools you may have installed and forgotten.
Check whether updates are automatic on the router, cameras, laptops and phones.
Check whether the account that manages everything is separate from the everyday account.
Check whether backups are off the device and whether you have ever restored one.
defensive: Turn on automatic updates everywhere, and prioritise the devices that face the internet.
Use a password manager and a separate, generated password for every account, with multi-factor on email first.
Do not expose remote access to anything; use a brokered service that does not require inbound connections.
Keep two backups, one of them offline, and test a restore once a year.
Write down what to do first if something goes wrong, so you are not deciding it while panicking.

topics.name: Careers and Specialisations (and What to Learn Next)
topics.description: What security roles actually involve, why job titles are the unreliable part, and how to choose a direction without a salary chart or a promise.

content.overview: Security is not one job. It splits into technical specialisms, into defensive and offensive work, and into the part of the job that is deciding what to do about it. Knowing which of those you are is more useful than a list of job titles.
how_it_works: The main technical families are security operations, security engineering, application security, and governance and risk.
Offensive work exists as a legitimate career, but the entry routes and the required judgement are different from defensive work.
Most roles are a mixture of technical and non-technical, and the non-technical half is what determines whether the technical half gets used.
The specialisms are converging: cloud, identity and supply chain have blurred the boundaries between them.
Portability comes from fundamentals and from a verifiable way of demonstrating you have them.
history: The profession grew out of system administration and network engineering, and that grounding still shows.
Consulting and audit created a separate non-technical track that never had a technical equivalent.
Cloud platforms moved the centre of gravity from the data centre to the identity provider.
Current hiring increasingly asks for demonstrable hands-on work, and less for credentials alone.
real_world: A generalist who can read code, configure a platform and write a policy is more employable than a narrow specialist in one of them.
A technical finding nobody communicates does not change anything, and that is the most common reason good security work is undervalued.
Someone who only has certification knowledge struggles once the environment does not match the exam.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the role involves the work you would rather do, since titles vary and descriptions often do not.
Check whether you would be expected to communicate with non-technical stakeholders, because most roles are.
Check whether the team actually has the authority to fix what it finds.
Check whether the role has a path, or whether it is the same job with more years.
defensive: Learn the fundamentals properly: operating systems, networking, and how identity actually works.
Demonstrate capability with something you built, broke and explained, rather than with a list of credentials.
Practise writing: a clear finding or a short design note is a genuine differentiator.
Get comfortable with the business language, since you will need to prioritise in those terms.
Pick a specialism deliberately after a broad base, rather than specialising before you know what the work involves.

topics.name: Certifications and How to Choose Them Honestly
topics.description: A credential is a claim about evidence, not about capability. How to tell what one asserts, what it does not, and whether the job you want even asks for it.

content.overview: Certifications help in some hiring contexts and hurt in others. The useful question is not which is best, but which one your target employers actually ask for, because that varies sharply by role and by country.
how_it_works: Some certifications are genuinely requirements: government clearance, contract bids, and regulated roles often name them explicitly.
Others are signals, and are read as evidence of effort rather than of capability.
A certification cannot demonstrate judgement, which is the thing the profession actually selects for.
Practical assessments test more than multiple choice, and generally carry more weight with hiring managers.
An expired certificate is worse than none in some procurement contexts, so the maintenance cost is part of the price.
history: Vendor-neutral entry certifications created a floor and made the field accessible without a degree.
Hands-on offensive certifications emerged to address the gap between knowing about exploitation and being able to do it.
Cloud platform certifications grew quickly with the platforms themselves.
The market consolidated around a smaller set of widely recognised names, which helped employers and hurt diversity of route.
real_world: A consultant bidding on a government contract may be unable to proceed without a named certification.
A senior engineering candidate is usually judged on evidence of work rather than on a certificate.
A certification obtained without ever using the material fails the first time the environment differs from the exam.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the role, the contract or the regulation names the certification explicitly.
Check what the exam actually tests, and whether it resembles the work you would be doing.
Check the renewal and continuing-education requirements, since they are a real ongoing cost.
Check how many people in the roles you want hold it, since a rare certificate is a weak signal.
defensive: Read the job description of the role you want and take the names from there rather than from a ranking.
Use certifications to fill a specific gap, not as the whole of your preparation.
Pair any certification with hands-on evidence, because the two together are much stronger than either alone.
Factor the renewal cost into the decision before you start, not after.
Be honest in interviews about what the certificate did and did not teach you.

topics.name: Building a Home Lab and Practising Safely
topics.description: Isolated, authorised, disposable: how to build a practice environment that stays safe, and the rules that keep every exercise inside a boundary you are allowed to be in.

content.overview: A home lab is where security understanding actually forms. It is also where care is needed, because a badly isolated lab is a real risk to the network it sits on.
how_it_works: The lab needs deliberately vulnerable targets, and they are built for exactly this and are safe by design when isolated.
Isolation is the whole point: host-only networking with no route to anything you care about.
Snapshots and templates make reset instant, which removes the temptation to test on something real.
Attack simulation on a lab host is a genuinely useful way to practise detection and response as well as offence.
Documentation of the lab is part of the lab, because an undocumented lab cannot be rebuilt or improved.
history: Labs were assembled by hand from old software and an isolated network segment, which was effective and slow.
Prebuilt vulnerable applications and environments removed most of the setup cost.
Virtualisation on ordinary laptops made it possible to run several systems at once.
Current practice increasingly defines the lab as code, so it is reproducible rather than bespoke.
real_world: A virtual machine with default bridged networking can reach the home network, which defeats the isolation entirely.
A lab machine running as administrator makes any mistake on it far worse.
A lab that is never reset accumulates state that makes later practice unreliable and misleading.
what_to_look_for: Check whether the lab network can route to your real network, and verify rather than trust the default.
Check what privileges the lab host account has.
Check whether you can reset quickly, and how long a rebuild takes.
Check whether the targets you are using are still maintained, since old images accumulate known issues.
defensive: Use host-only or a dedicated internal network, and confirm isolation from inside the lab.
Run the lab host as a standard, unprivileged user.
Snapshot before each session and keep at least one clean template.
Take the lab offline entirely when it is not in use, which removes the risk rather than managing it.
Write down how to rebuild it, so the lab survives a machine failure and stays trustworthy.

topics.name: Where This Ends: Your Next Specialisation
topics.description: An honest map of what this foundation covers, what it deliberately does not, and where the specialisation categories begin.

content.overview: This is the end of the fundamentals, not the end of the subject. What you do next depends on which part of it you enjoyed, and that is a better signal than any roadmap.
how_it_works: The fundamentals give you the vocabulary to read a finding, judge a risk and argue for a control without help.
Every specialism here assumes them, which is why they are worth learning before choosing.
The next step is depth in one area plus continued breadth, because the specialisms keep recombining.
Keeping a record of what you actually built and fixed is worth more than any of the resources you consume.
Security changes quickly enough that the habit of learning is the part that has to last.
history: The field has repeatedly split into new specialisms and then recombined, so a chosen path is rarely permanent.
Cloud, identity and supply chain have merged several traditional boundaries within a few years.
Certification structures have changed less than the underlying work has.
The fundamentals have stayed remarkably stable even as everything around them has moved.
real_world: Someone who enjoyed the systems lessons goes towards security engineering; someone who enjoyed the risk lessons goes towards governance.
A person who found the offensive material most interesting often ends up in detection engineering, which surprises them.
The most valuable next step for most people is applying one thing properly rather than sampling everything.
what_to_look_for: Notice which lessons you wanted to keep reading, because that is the most reliable signal available to you.
Check whether you can explain a real finding in your own environment now, which is the practical test of this material.
Check whether you can say what you would do differently in your own systems, since that is the point of it.
Check whether you have something you built, since that is what makes the next step possible.
defensive: Go deep in the area that held your attention, and keep a little breadth everywhere else.
Apply one thing properly: harden a system, run a test, or write a plan, and finish it.
Keep a written record of what you did and what happened, since that record is what evidences capability.
Follow one authoritative source per topic rather than many shallow ones.
Come back to these fundamentals whenever a specialism starts feeling unmoored, because they are the reference frame.

topics.name: Web Application Security Fundamentals
topics.description: A practical introduction to web application security: assets, users, trust boundaries, attack surface, and the difference between a bug and a security vulnerability.

content.seo_title: Web Application Security Fundamentals: Beginner Guide | OopsMyPassword
content.seo_description: Learn web application security fundamentals, attack surface, trust boundaries, security controls, and a practical testing mindset.
content.overview: Web application security is the practice of designing, building, testing, and operating web applications so that untrusted users cannot cross security boundaries they are not authorized to cross. Identify important assets, identify who can influence each request, map trust boundaries, and verify every security-sensitive decision on the server. A web bug becomes a security issue when it lets an untrusted party violate confidentiality, integrity, authentication, authorization, or availability.
how_it_works: Start with the application model: browser or client → web server → application logic → database or internal service.
Map assets and actions: accounts, personal data, administrative functions, files, payments, tokens, and other sensitive operations.
Treat browser-controlled values, cookies, headers, URL parameters, request bodies, and client-side JavaScript as potentially attacker-controlled.
Find the security decision: is this user logged in, can this user edit this record, or is this value safe to pass to another interpreter?
Verify the decision at the trusted server-side boundary. Hiding a button in the browser is not an authorization control.
content.history: Web security evolved from simple server-rendered pages into distributed applications with browsers, APIs, databases, CDNs, identity providers, third-party JavaScript, and cloud services. OWASP Top 10:2025 is an awareness baseline rather than a complete security standard; OWASP recommends ASVS when teams need verifiable application-security requirements.
real_world: OWASP Top 10:2025 puts Broken Access Control at A01 and Authentication Failures at A07, showing how central identity and authorization are to application security.

Modern applications combine multiple trust boundaries: browser state, reverse proxies, application servers, databases, object storage, and third-party services. A security control is useful only if the component making the final decision actually trusts the data it uses.
what_to_look_for: List sensitive assets and privileged actions before testing.
Identify every user-controlled input and where it is consumed.
Check whether authentication, authorization, validation, and security-sensitive business rules are enforced server-side.
Compare what the UI allows with what the underlying HTTP endpoints actually accept.
Look for inconsistent security controls between similar endpoints, methods, roles, or application states.
defensive: Use a documented threat model and explicit trust boundaries.
Centralize authentication and authorization decisions where practical.
Deny access by default for protected resources and fail securely.
Validate and normalize security-sensitive input at the point of use.
Log important authentication and authorization failures without leaking secrets.
Use OWASP ASVS when you need a testable security-requirements baseline rather than relying on the Top 10 alone.

topics.name: HTTP Requests & Responses
topics.description: Understand HTTP methods, URLs, headers, cookies, status codes, request bodies, and why HTTP is the foundation of practical web security testing.

content.seo_title: HTTP Requests & Responses for Web Security | OopsMyPassword
content.seo_description: Learn HTTP requests and responses for web security testing: methods, headers, cookies, status codes, parameters, and request flow.
content.overview: HTTP is the language through which browsers and web applications exchange requests and responses. For security testing, read the HTTP message rather than treating a web page as a black box. A request can contain a method, path, query parameters, headers, cookies, and a body. A response can contain a status code, headers, cookies, and content. Small differences often reveal authentication, authorization, caching, validation, or routing behavior.
how_it_works: The client sends a request such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE to a URL.
The request can contain query parameters, headers, cookies, and a body. Treat values supplied by the client as untrusted unless the server independently verifies them.
A server or intermediary processes the request and returns a response with a status code, headers, cookies, and content.
Cookies can make stateless HTTP participate in stateful sessions, so security depends on how session identifiers are generated, transmitted, scoped, and invalidated.
Reverse proxies, CDNs, and caches can introduce additional parsing and trust boundaries, so the same request should not automatically be assumed to mean the same thing at every layer.
content.history: HTTP originated as a simple protocol for transferring hypermedia and has evolved through HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. Its headers, methods, caching behavior, cookies, authentication mechanisms, and proxy ecosystem are fundamental to modern applications.
real_world: MDN describes HTTP as a client-server protocol where clients send requests and servers return responses; understanding that flow is foundational for web debugging and security testing.
Security issues such as request smuggling, cache poisoning, authentication weaknesses, and Host-header problems can arise when different components interpret HTTP messages differently.
what_to_look_for: Identify the method, path, query string, Host header, cookies, authorization headers, content type, and body.
Record how status codes and response bodies change when one input changes.
Check which values are reflected, stored, used for routing, used for authorization, or passed to another component.
Compare browser-visible behavior with the underlying request and response.
Pay attention to Set-Cookie attributes such as Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite.
defensive: Use HTTPS consistently and configure secure transport correctly.
Parse and validate HTTP messages consistently across front-end and back-end components.
Set appropriate cookie attributes and avoid placing sensitive data in URLs when a safer mechanism is available.
Return appropriate status codes without exposing unnecessary implementation details.
Define explicit cache behavior for sensitive responses and test proxy/CDN behavior.
Use a well-tested framework HTTP stack rather than implementing protocol parsing yourself.

topics.name: Authentication & Session Security
topics.description: Learn how websites verify identity, maintain sessions, handle passwords and MFA, and where authentication logic can fail.

content.seo_title: Web Authentication & Session Security Guide | OopsMyPassword
content.seo_description: Learn secure web authentication and session management: login flows, cookies, MFA, password reset, brute-force protection, and common weaknesses.
content.overview: Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you are allowed to do. Authentication normally involves a credential or factor, a verification step, and then a session mechanism that lets the application recognize subsequent requests. Failures can appear in login, password reset, MFA, remember-me features, session handling, logout, or recovery flows—not only in the main login form.
how_it_works: A user submits an authentication attempt, usually over HTTPS.
The server verifies the supplied factor against trusted credential or identity data.
After successful authentication, the application establishes a session using a secure session identifier or another validated mechanism.
Subsequent requests carry the session state, commonly through a cookie, and the server maps it to the authenticated identity.
Sensitive state changes such as login, privilege changes, password changes, and recovery should trigger appropriate session lifecycle controls.
content.history: Web authentication progressed from simple HTTP authentication and password forms toward cookie-based sessions, federated identity, MFA, passkeys, and modern identity protocols. The larger the authentication surface becomes, the more important consistent session lifecycle and recovery controls become.
real_world: PortSwigger's current authentication material covers username enumeration, brute-force defenses, MFA logic, password reset, remember-me mechanisms, and other authentication flaws.

OWASP ASVS 5.0 separates authentication and session management into dedicated verification areas, reflecting that proving identity and securely maintaining that identity are related but distinct controls.
what_to_look_for: Check whether invalid and valid usernames produce distinguishable messages, status codes, response sizes, or timing.
Review login rate limiting and whether recovery or password-change endpoints have weaker controls than the main login.
Inspect session cookies for appropriate security attributes and check whether sessions are rotated at important authentication boundaries.
Review logout, password reset, remember-me, MFA, and re-authentication flows as separate attack surfaces.
Look for state-machine flaws where an application grants authenticated functionality before every required verification step is complete.
defensive: Use HTTPS for authentication and enforce secure transport.
Use a well-tested authentication framework and store passwords using modern password hashing rather than reversible encryption.
Use generic authentication error responses and sensible abuse controls without creating account-enumeration leaks.
Generate unpredictable session identifiers and rotate them after authentication or other sensitive state transitions.
Protect session cookies with appropriate Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite settings.
Make password reset, MFA, remember-me, and account recovery at least as carefully protected as normal login.

topics.name: Access Control & Authorization
topics.description: Learn how web applications decide which users can access which data and perform which actions, including horizontal and vertical privilege boundaries.

content.seo_title: Web Access Control & Authorization: IDOR and Privilege Escalation | OopsMyPassword
content.seo_description: Learn web access control and authorization, including horizontal and vertical privilege escalation, IDOR/BOLA concepts, and secure authorization design.
content.overview: Access control is the server-side decision about whether an already-identified user is allowed to access a resource or perform an action. A strong authorization model considers identity, role, resource, action, and context. Common failures include horizontal access-control problems where one user can access another user's data, and vertical privilege escalation where a lower-privileged user reaches administrative functionality.
how_it_works: Authentication establishes the identity associated with a request.
The application determines the requested resource and action.
The server evaluates policy using trusted identity and authorization data.
The server allows or denies the operation. The decision must happen at the protected resource or action, not only in the UI.
For object-level access, the authorization check must bind the requested object to the caller's actual permissions or ownership.
content.history: As web applications moved from simple pages to multi-user systems and APIs, authorization became a major security boundary. OWASP Top 10:2025 lists Broken Access Control as A01. Modern ASVS 5.0 includes dedicated authorization requirements covering general authorization design, operation-level authorization, and other authorization considerations.
real_world: PortSwigger's access-control material covers vertical and horizontal privilege escalation, IDOR, multi-step processes, URL and method-based controls, and prevention.

OWASP guidance emphasizes explicit authorization checks for each protected resource or action rather than relying on obscurity, client-side controls, or assumptions about how users navigate the application.
what_to_look_for: Create a matrix of roles, users, resources, and sensitive actions.
Compare the same request using two authorized test accounts with different ownership or privilege levels.
Check direct object references such as user IDs, document IDs, order IDs, filenames, and account identifiers.
Test protected functions through their underlying HTTP requests rather than relying on whether a button is visible.
Review multi-step workflows and alternate HTTP methods for inconsistent authorization enforcement.
defensive: Deny access by default to protected resources.
Enforce authorization server-side at the point where the resource or action is accessed.
Centralize authorization policy where practical so endpoints do not implement contradictory rules.
Bind object access to the authenticated principal and explicit permissions; never trust a client-supplied role or ownership field.
Test horizontal, vertical, and context-dependent authorization paths with negative cases.
Log important authorization failures and review them for abuse patterns.

topics.name: SQL Injection & Parameterized Queries
topics.description: Understand how string concatenation turns user input into database commands, and why prepared statements keep code and data separate.

content.seo_title: SQL Injection & Parameterized Queries | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Learn how SQL injection happens when input is concatenated into queries and how parameterized prepared statements prevent it.
content.overview: SQL injection (SQLi) occurs when an application builds a database query by concatenating untrusted input directly into the SQL command string. Because the database parser cannot tell where the developer’s query ends and the user’s data begins, crafted characters can alter query logic, bypass checks, read unauthorized rows, or modify data. The primary defense is structural: parameterized queries (prepared statements) compile the SQL structure first and pass user values separately as bound parameters.
how_it_works: An application receives input from a query parameter, form field, header, cookie, or stored record.
If the code concatenates that input into a raw SQL string, characters like quotes, operators, or SQL keywords are parsed as part of the command syntax.
In-band SQLi returns results directly in the page; blind SQLi infers answers from boolean page differences or database response delays.
With a parameterized query, the database compiles the statement template ahead of time and treats the bound parameter strictly as a literal value, never as executable SQL syntax.
content.history: First documented widely in Phrack Magazine in 1998, SQL injection has remained one of the most damaging web vulnerability classes for over two decades despite having a clear, universal engineering fix.
real_world: High-profile breaches have repeatedly traced back to legacy endpoints or dynamic ORDER BY / filter clauses where developers bypassed query parameterization.
Even modern ORM frameworks can expose SQL injection when raw query helpers or string interpolation are used for dynamic table or column names.
what_to_look_for: Search codebases for string interpolation or concatenation inside SQL query builders and raw ORM query calls.
Check dynamic sorting, filtering, and search endpoints where column names or directions cannot use standard value placeholders.
Verify that database error messages and stack traces are logged internally rather than returned in HTTP responses.
defensive: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for every variable data value in SQL statements.
Validate dynamic identifiers such as column names or sort orders against a strict server-side allowlist.
Run the application database connection with least-privilege credentials limited to required tables and operations.
Avoid exposing raw database driver errors to clients.

topics.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Contexts & CSP
topics.description: Learn how reflected and stored XSS execute scripts in a victim’s browser, why output context matters, and how Content Security Policy reduces impact.

content.seo_title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Contexts & CSP | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Understand reflected and stored XSS, context-aware output encoding for HTML, attributes, URLs, and scripts, plus Content Security Policy.
content.overview: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) happens when an application includes untrusted data in a web page without proper encoding or validation for the specific browser context where it appears. When a victim’s browser renders the page, it executes the injected JavaScript within the origin of the trusted site—allowing the script to read page data, make authenticated requests, or alter the UI.
how_it_works: In reflected XSS, untrusted input from the current HTTP request (such as a search query) is echoed immediately into the HTML response.
In stored XSS, untrusted input (such as a comment, profile bio, or support ticket) is saved on the server and rendered later to other users or administrators.
Each output location in a document—HTML body text, HTML attribute, URL attribute (href/src), or inline JavaScript—is parsed differently by the browser.
Context-aware output encoding converts characters that have special meaning in that specific context into safe literal representations before the browser parses them.
content.history: Coined in the early 2000s as "cross-site scripting" to describe loading scripts across domains, XSS quickly became the most common vulnerability reported in bug bounty programs worldwide.
real_world: Stored XSS in customer support dashboards or admin panels can silently compromise privileged staff sessions when they view an attacker-submitted record.
HTML entity encoding inside an href="javascript:..." attribute does not stop script execution because the browser decodes attributes before evaluating the URL scheme.
what_to_look_for: Identify every place where user-controlled strings are rendered into HTML templates, attributes, or links.
Check user-supplied URLs (such as profile website links or avatar URLs) to ensure only http: and https: schemes are permitted.
Inspect whether templates disable auto-escaping (for example, raw HTML directives) on user content.
defensive: Use modern templating engines or UI frameworks that automatically apply context-aware encoding by default.
Validate URLs rendered into href or src attributes so only safe schemes (https:, http:, or site-relative paths) are allowed.
Set HttpOnly on session cookies so injected JavaScript cannot read raw session identifiers via document.cookie.
Deploy a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) that blocks inline script execution and restricts script sources.

topics.name: DOM-Based Vulnerabilities & Sanitization
topics.description: Trace client-side sources and sinks in browser JavaScript, understand why innerHTML is dangerous, and sanitize rich HTML safely.

content.seo_title: DOM XSS, Sinks & HTML Sanitization | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Learn how DOM-based XSS flows from client-side sources like location.search to sinks like innerHTML, and how textContent and sanitizers prevent it.
content.overview: DOM-based vulnerabilities occur entirely inside browser JavaScript when code reads data from an untrusted client-side source (such as location.search, location.hash, or postMessage) and passes it into a dangerous DOM sink (such as element.innerHTML, document.write, or location.assign) without safe handling. Even if the server never sees the payload, the browser executes it in the application’s origin.
how_it_works: A source is any browser property or API that an attacker can influence, including URL query strings, URL fragments, referrer headers, storage entries, or cross-window messages.
A sink is a browser DOM property or function that interprets strings as HTML markup, executable code, or navigation targets.
When JavaScript assigns untrusted text to innerHTML or outerHTML, the browser parses embedded tags and event handlers (such as ).
Using textContent or createElement assigns plain text nodes that the browser never parses as HTML markup.
content.history: As single-page applications shifted rendering logic from server templates to client-side JavaScript in the 2010s, DOM-based XSS grew from a niche edge case into a primary web security focus.
real_world: Client-side search widgets and tab routers frequently read location.hash or query parameters and inject them directly into a status banner via innerHTML.
Window postMessage listeners that fail to check event.origin can allow any third-party tab to send commands or markup into the page.
what_to_look_for: Audit assignments to innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, and Function.
Check window.addEventListener("message", ...) handlers for strict event.origin verification.
Review client-side redirects that read returnUrl or next parameters from the URL and pass them to location.href.
defensive: Use textContent, setAttribute, and DOM node creation APIs instead of innerHTML whenever rendering plain text.
When rich HTML or Markdown rendering is required, pass output through a vetted allowlist HTML sanitizer before inserting it into the DOM.
Validate redirect targets against same-origin paths before calling location.assign or location.replace.
Adopt browser Trusted Types where supported to block raw string assignments to dangerous DOM sinks.

topics.name: CSRF, SameSite Cookies & State-Changing Requests
topics.description: See how Cross-Site Request Forgery abuses ambient browser cookies and how CSRF tokens, SameSite attributes, and method discipline stop it.

content.seo_title: CSRF Defense & SameSite Cookies | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Understand Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), why browsers attach cookies automatically, and how anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies protect state changes.
content.overview: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks a victim’s browser into sending an unintended state-changing request—such as changing an email address, transferring funds, or rotating an API key—to a site where the victim is currently signed in. Because browsers automatically attach session cookies to cross-site requests unless restricted, the server may treat the forged request as a genuine action by the user.
how_it_works: A user signs into a web application and receives a session cookie stored by their browser.
While that session is active, the user visits another page or opens an email containing a hidden form or script that submits a request to the target application.
If the session cookie lacks SameSite protection and the endpoint requires no unpredictable request token, the browser sends the cookie and the server executes the action.
An anti-CSRF token (or custom header verified on the server) works because a cross-origin page cannot read the token from the target origin due to the Same-Origin Policy.
content.history: Historically widespread across form-based web apps, CSRF prompted browser vendors to change the default cookie behavior to SameSite=Lax, dramatically reducing accidental exposure while keeping explicit anti-CSRF tokens essential for sensitive endpoints.
real_world: Applications that perform state changes on GET requests (such as /account/delete?confirm=1) remain vulnerable even with SameSite=Lax cookies because top-level link navigations still send Lax cookies.
Login CSRF can bind a victim’s browser to an attacker-controlled account so the victim inadvertently saves sensitive data into the attacker’s profile.
what_to_look_for: Verify that GET and HEAD requests are strictly read-only and never mutate server state.
Check whether state-changing POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE endpoints validate a cryptographic anti-CSRF token or require a non-simple custom header with strict CORS.
Inspect Set-Cookie headers to confirm SameSite=Lax or SameSite=Strict is explicitly set.
defensive: Require unpredictable, session-bound anti-CSRF tokens on all state-changing form and API requests.
Never perform state-changing operations on GET requests.
Explicitly set SameSite=Lax (or SameSite=Strict for high-sensitivity sessions) along with Secure and HttpOnly on session cookies.
Verify the Origin or Referer header on sensitive state-changing requests as an additional defense-in-depth check.

topics.name: SSRF & Outbound Request Controls
topics.description: Learn how Server-Side Request Forgery tricks a server into fetching internal network resources or cloud metadata, and how to isolate outbound calls.

content.seo_title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Defense | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Learn how SSRF vulnerabilities let attackers reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints, and how allowlists and network isolation prevent them.
content.overview: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) happens when an application fetches a remote resource using a URL or hostname supplied or influenced by a user without verifying the destination. Because the request originates from the trusted application server, an attacker can use it to reach internal-only services, loopback interfaces, private RFC 1918 networks, or cloud instance metadata endpoints.
how_it_works: Features such as webhook testers, URL link previews, PDF generators, and remote avatar importers ask the server to fetch a URL.
If the server accepts arbitrary URLs, an attacker can supply internal addresses like http://127.0.0.1, internal admin hostnames, or cloud metadata IPs (169.254.169.254).
Even if the application only validates the initial URL string, HTTP 302 redirects or DNS rebinding can point the actual socket connection at a private IP address.
Effective defense combines application-layer allowlisting, DNS resolution validation at connection time, and network-layer egress isolation.
content.history: SSRF rose to prominence with cloud computing and microservice architectures, earning its own dedicated category in the OWASP Top 10 (A10:2021) due to its role in major cloud credential thefts.
real_world: Cloud metadata services on link-local addresses (169.254.169.254) have been queried via SSRF to extract temporary IAM role credentials when metadata session tokens were not required.
Server-side HTML-to-PDF converters that evaluate embedded <iframe> or <link> tags frequently act as hidden SSRF vectors.
what_to_look_for: Identify any endpoint that accepts a full URL, domain name, webhook target, or file import link from the client.
Check whether the HTTP client follows redirects automatically to unvalidated destinations.
Verify whether cloud instances enforce session-oriented metadata access (such as IMDSv2) and restrict outbound connections.
defensive: Avoid fetching user-supplied URLs from application servers whenever possible; prefer strict allowlists of known partner domains.
Resolve hostnames and block connections to loopback, link-local, and private IP ranges at the custom socket/dialer layer, and disable automatic HTTP redirects.
Route legitimate user-initiated fetches through an isolated egress proxy in a dedicated network segment with no access to internal services.
Require token-authenticated cloud metadata endpoints (such as AWS IMDSv2) and minimize instance IAM privileges.

topics.name: File Upload Validation & Storage Isolation
topics.description: Design safe file upload pipelines: why filename extensions and Content-Type headers cannot be trusted, and how to isolate stored files.

content.seo_title: Secure File Uploads & Storage Isolation | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Learn how file upload vulnerabilities lead to stored XSS, path traversal, or server execution, and how to validate and isolate uploaded files.
content.overview: File upload features accept complex binary or text streams directly from untrusted clients. If an application trusts the client-supplied filename, Content-Type header, or file contents, attackers may upload active web scripts, SVG documents containing JavaScript, oversized archive bombs, or path-traversal filenames that overwrite sensitive files.
how_it_works: The browser sends a multipart/form-data request containing a filename, a Content-Type header, and raw bytes—all of which are controlled by the client.
If the server saves the file using the raw user filename inside a web-accessible directory, an uploaded .html, .svg, or server script may be executed when requested.
Even image uploads can carry embedded scripts if the server or browser sniffs the content as HTML or SVG on the main application origin.
