Generating a random UUID filename, verifying magic bytes/dimensions, and serving user files from a separate cookieless storage domain neutralizes these risks.
content.history: Unrestricted file upload has been a classic path to full server compromise or stored XSS since early bulletin boards and content management systems stored uploads in executable web roots.
real_world: Uploaded SVG avatars rendered inline on the main application domain execute embedded <script> tags with full access to the user’s session.
Filenames containing ../ sequences in multipart uploads or zip archives (Zip Slip) can write files outside the intended upload folder.
what_to_look_for: Check whether uploaded filenames are stripped or replaced with server-generated random identifiers.
Test whether SVG or HTML files can be uploaded and viewed directly on the main application origin.
Verify that responses serving user downloads include X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and safe Content-Disposition headers.
defensive: Never use client-supplied filenames on disk or in object keys; generate random UUID filenames and allowlist safe extensions.
Verify file signatures (magic bytes) and re-encode or validate images server-side; enforce strict file size limits.
Store uploads outside the application web root—ideally in an isolated object storage bucket served from a separate, cookieless domain.
Serve user downloads with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

topics.name: Security Headers, CORS & TLS Deployment
topics.description: Configure browser security headers, understand the Same-Origin Policy and CORS misconfigurations, and enforce HTTPS with HSTS.

content.seo_title: HTTP Security Headers, CORS & HSTS Guide | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Master browser security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, nosniff), Same-Origin Policy, and how to avoid dangerous CORS misconfigurations.
content.overview: Browsers enforce powerful built-in isolation through the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) and optional HTTP response headers. However, overly permissive Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) headers or missing transport and framing headers can weaken those protections, exposing authenticated API responses or allowing clickjacking and downgrade attacks.
how_it_works: The Same-Origin Policy prevents scripts on one origin (scheme + host + port) from reading responses from another origin unless the server explicitly opts in via CORS headers.
If an API reflects an arbitrary Origin header in Access-Control-Allow-Origin while also setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, any website can read authenticated responses.
Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) instructs browsers to connect only over HTTPS, preventing protocol downgrade and cookie hijacking on untrusted networks.
Frame restrictions (CSP frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options) stop attackers from embedding a sensitive page inside an invisible iframe to trick users into clicking buttons (clickjacking).
content.history: Introduced by Netscape in 1995, the Same-Origin Policy remains the cornerstone of web browser isolation, supplemented over time by CORS, HSTS, CSP, and Fetch Metadata headers.
real_world: APIs that dynamically reflect req.headers.origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Allow-Credentials: true effectively disable the Same-Origin Policy for signed-in users.
Weak regex checks on Origin headers (such as matching *example.com without anchoring) have allowed attackers to register evil-example.com and steal account data.
what_to_look_for: Inspect HTTP responses for Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and Referrer-Policy.
Test CORS behavior by sending requests with an arbitrary Origin header and checking whether it is reflected with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
Confirm that framing is restricted via frame-ancestors in CSP or X-Frame-Options.
defensive: Compare incoming Origin headers against an exact allowlist of trusted origins; never reflect arbitrary origins when Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is true.
Enable HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) and redirect all HTTP traffic permanently to HTTPS.
Set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and frame-ancestors restrictions on all responses.
Review Permissions-Policy to disable unused browser features such as camera, microphone, and geolocation.

topics.name: API Rate Limiting, Logging & Defensive Verification
topics.description: Protect web APIs against automated abuse, design privacy-safe security audit logs, and verify security controls continuously in CI.

content.seo_title: API Rate Limiting, Security Logging & Testing | OMP Academy
content.seo_description: Learn how to defend web APIs with layered rate limiting, structured security logging without leaking secrets, and automated regression testing.
content.overview: Even when an application has no classic injection or XSS flaws, attackers target business logic and API endpoints with automated credential stuffing, OTP brute-forcing, scraping, and resource exhaustion. Production resilience requires layered rate limiting, structured audit logging that never records plaintext secrets, and automated security regression tests.
how_it_works: Automated bots send thousands of requests per minute across rotating IP addresses to test leaked credentials, guess reset codes, or exhaust expensive endpoints.
Layered rate limiting tracks request budgets per IP, per account identifier, and per endpoint cost so neither a single host nor a distributed botnet can brute-force a target account.
Security audit logs record authentication outcomes, privilege changes, and authorization denials with correlation IDs—while explicitly redacting passwords, tokens, and session cookies.
Automated integration tests in CI assert that unauthenticated and cross-tenant requests receive 401/403 responses before code ships.
content.history: As modern applications moved to JSON APIs and mobile clients, OWASP introduced the dedicated API Security Top 10 to address resource consumption, broken object-level authorization, and automated abuse.
real_world: Password reset endpoints that accept a 4- or 6-digit numeric code without per-account attempt limits can be brute-forced in seconds across multiple IP addresses.
Debug loggers that dump raw HTTP headers or request bodies into central log indices have accidentally exposed bearer tokens and plaintext passwords to internal readers.
what_to_look_for: Check login, MFA verification, password reset, and coupon/checkout endpoints for per-account and per-IP rate limits.
Verify that security logs capture failed logins and access-control denials without logging passwords, session cookies, or API keys.
Confirm that CI pipelines include automated tests for authorization boundaries, SEO/CSP headers, and dependency vulnerabilities.
defensive: Enforce both per-IP and per-account rate limits and short lockouts or exponential backoff on authentication, MFA, and recovery endpoints.
Use short-lived, high-entropy tokens for password resets and invalidate them immediately after use or after a small number of failed attempts.
Log security-relevant events in a structured format with automatic redaction of Authorization headers, cookies, and password fields.
Write automated unit and integration tests for access control rules so regressions fail the build before deployment.

labs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
labs.description: Explore reflected and stored XSS contexts and test how output encoding and Content Security Policy mitigate script injection.

labs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: DOM-Based Vulnerabilities
labs.description: Trace client-side sources and DOM sinks in interactive browser labs and compare unsafe innerHTML with safe DOM APIs.

labs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
labs.description: Understand how cross-site requests abuse session cookies and how anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite attributes protect state-changing endpoints.

labs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
labs.description: See how outbound server requests can be redirected toward internal services and how allowlists and network isolation prevent SSRF.

labs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: File Upload Vulnerabilities
labs.description: Learn why content-type headers and file extensions cannot be trusted alone and how to isolate uploaded files safely.

labs.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: CORS & Security Headers
labs.description: Explore Same-Origin Policy boundaries, CORS origin reflection mistakes, and clickjacking defenses.

labs.title: OWASP API Security Project & Cheat Sheets
labs.description: Review OWASP guidance on API rate limiting, authentication brute-force controls, and structured security logging.
